options.text: Set up all read replicas in a different region using asynchronous replication.
Set up all read replicas in the same region as the primary instance with synchronous replication.
Set up read replicas in different zones of the same region as the primary instance with synchronous replication, and set up read replicas in different regions with asynchronous replication.
Set up read replicas in different zones of the same region as the primary instance with asynchronous replication, and set up read replicas in different regions with synchronous replication.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL high availability uses synchronous replication across zones within a region, so a zonal failover can occur without data loss. Cross-region replicas provide disaster-recovery capability for a regional outage, but their replication is asynchronous; replication lag determines the possible data-loss window during regional recovery.

**Learn more:** [About high availability | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/high-availability) · [Promote replicas for regional migration or disaster recovery | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/replication/cross-region-replicas)

Your company is building a global ecommerce website on Google Cloud. The development team is creating a shopping-cart service that must be durable and elastically scalable under live traffic. Business disruption from unplanned downtime must remain below 5 minutes per month. Additionally, the application requires very low-latency writes. You need a data-storage solution with high write throughput and 99.99% uptime. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud SQL for data storage.
Use Cloud Spanner for data storage.
Use Memorystore for data storage.
Use Bigtable for data storage.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Spanner is a horizontally scalable, strongly consistent ACID database suited to durable ecommerce transaction data such as shopping carts. A regional Spanner instance has a 99.99% monthly uptime SLA, satisfying the less-than-five-minutes-per-month availability target, and Spanner scales compute and storage to support high write throughput. Multi-region configurations can provide even higher availability when required.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Spanner Service Level Agreement (SLA)](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/sla) · [Cloud Spanner: Always-on, virtually unlimited scale database](https://cloud.google.com/spanner)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing a highly available (HA) Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance for use by 100 databases. Each database contains 80 tables migrated from your on-premises environment to Google Cloud. The applications that use these databases run in multiple US regions, and you must ensure low latency for both read and write operations. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy 2 Cloud SQL instances in the us-central1 region with HA enabled, and create read replicas in us-east1 and us-west1.
Deploy 2 Cloud SQL instances in the us-central1 region, and create read replicas in us-east1 and us-west1.
Deploy 4 Cloud SQL instances in the us-central1 region with HA enabled, and create read replicas in us-central1, us-east1, and us-west1.
Deploy 4 Cloud SQL instances in the us-central1 region, and create read replicas in us-central1, us-east1 and us-west1.

questions.explanation:
A regional Cloud SQL HA configuration provides a primary and standby across separate zones, enabling automatic failover and preserving availability for writes. Cross-region read replicas in `us-east1` and `us-west1` place read capacity nearer to applications in those regions, which improves read latency while the HA primary handles writes in its configured region.

**Learn more:** [About high availability | Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/high-availability) · [About replication in Cloud SQL | Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/replication)

questions.domain: Design scalable and highly available cloud database solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing a payments-processing application on Google Cloud. The application must keep serving requests and prevent user disruption if a regional failure happens. You need to use AES-256 to encrypt database data and want to control where the encryption key is stored. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Spanner with a customer-managed encryption key (CMEK).
Use Cloud Spanner with default encryption.
Use Cloud SQL with a customer-managed encryption key (CMEK).
Use Bigtable with default encryption.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Spanner multi-region configurations replicate data across regions and maintain availability during regional failures. Spanner supports customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) in Cloud KMS, which lets the customer control key location, lifecycle, permissions, and rotation. Cloud KMS symmetric encryption keys use AES-256.

**Learn more:** [Regional, dual-region, and multi-region configurations | Spanner](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/instance-configurations) · [Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) overview | Spanner](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/cmek)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are planning to migrate a large Oracle database to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL. The database contains a substantial amount of application logic in stored procedures that must be migrated to the target database. You want to minimize both the migration effort and migration downtime. What should you do?

options.text: Use Ora2pg for schema and code conversion and data migration.
Use Ora2pg for schema and code conversion. Use the oracle_fdw extension in AlloyDB and replicate data from source to destination by using CREATE TABLE AS SELECT statements.

Use Database Migration Service. Set up a conversion workspace for schema and code conversion. Create a migration job to perform backfill and change data capture to replicate data from source to destination.

Use Database Migration Service. Set up a legacy conversion workspace for schema and code conversion. Create a migration job to perform backfill and change data capture to replicate data from source to destination.

questions.explanation:
Database Migration Service conversion workspaces convert Oracle schema and supported code objects, including stored procedures, to PostgreSQL syntax. A continuous Database Migration Service job performs the initial data backfill and then uses change data capture (CDC) to keep AlloyDB synchronized until cutover, which reduces downtime. Legacy conversion workspaces are older, more limited, use Ora2Pg-based conversion, and are not recommended for migrations.

**Learn more:** [Conversion workspaces | Database Migration Service for heterogeneous Oracle to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/oracle-to-alloydb/about-conversion-workspaces) · [Create a migration job | Database Migration Service for heterogeneous Oracle to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/oracle-to-alloydb/create-migration-job)

As part of the high-availability and disaster-recovery design, the required recovery time objective (RTO) and recovery point objective (RPO) must be measured in minutes rather than hours. You need a high-availability configuration that can recover with no data loss during either a zonal or regional failure. What should you do?"}],"
",["$","$L55",null,{"choices":{"A":"Set up all read replicas in a different region using asynchronous replication.","B":"Set up all read replicas in the same region as the primary instance with synchronous replication.","C":"Set up read replicas in different zones of the same region as the primary instance with synchronous replication, and set up read replicas in different regions with asynchronous replication.","D":"Set up read replicas in different zones of the same region as the primary instance with asynchronous replication, and set up read replicas in different regions with synchronous replication."},"correctAnswer":"C","explanation":"Cloud SQL high availability uses synchronous replication across zones within a region, so a zonal failover can occur without data loss. Cross-region replicas provide disaster-recovery capability for a regional outage, but their replication is asynchronous; replication lag determines the possible data-loss window during regional recovery.

**Learn more:** [About high availability | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/high-availability) · [Promote replicas for regional migration or disaster recovery | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/replication/cross-region-replicas)","trackingInfo":{"questionId":"c1b0a9d1-a0ef-4f35-99a2-dc0398461f3b","examProvider":"google","examName":"professional-cloud-database-engineer","mode":"default"}}]]
51:[["$","p",null,{"children":"Your company is building a global ecommerce website on Google Cloud. The development team is creating a shopping-cart service that must be durable and elastically scalable under live traffic. Business disruption from unplanned downtime must remain below 5 minutes per month. Additionally, the application requires very low-latency writes. You need a data-storage solution with high write throughput and 99.99% uptime. What should you do?"}],"
",["$","$L55",null,{"choices":{"A":"Use Cloud SQL for data storage.","B":"Use Cloud Spanner for data storage.","C":"Use Memorystore for data storage.","D":"Use Bigtable for data storage."},"correctAnswer":"B","explanation":"Cloud Spanner is a horizontally scalable, strongly consistent ACID database suited to durable ecommerce transaction data such as shopping carts. A regional Spanner instance has a 99.99% monthly uptime SLA, satisfying the less-than-five-minutes-per-month availability target, and Spanner scales compute and storage to support high write throughput. Multi-region configurations can provide even higher availability when required.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Spanner Service Level Agreement (SLA)](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/sla) · [Cloud Spanner: Always-on, virtually unlimited scale database](https://cloud.google.com/spanner)","trackingInfo":{"questionId":"4eb25957-a605-4092-97b4-30560db8ddec","examProvider":"google","examName":"professional-cloud-database-engineer","mode":"default"}}]]
52:[["$","p",null,{"children":"You are designing a highly available (HA) Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance for use by 100 databases. Each database contains 80 tables migrated from your on-premises environment to Google Cloud. The applications that use these databases run in multiple US regions, and you must ensure low latency for both read and write operations. What should you do?"}],"
",["$","$L55",null,{"choices":{"A":"Deploy 2 Cloud SQL instances in the us-central1 region with HA enabled, and create read replicas in us-east1 and us-west1.","B":"Deploy 2 Cloud SQL instances in the us-central1 region, and create read replicas in us-east1 and us-west1.","C":"Deploy 4 Cloud SQL instances in the us-central1 region with HA enabled, and create read replicas in us-central1, us-east1, and us-west1.","D":"Deploy 4 Cloud SQL instances in the us-central1 region, and create read replicas in us-central1, us-east1 and us-west1."},"correctAnswer":"A","explanation":"A regional Cloud SQL HA configuration provides a primary and standby across separate zones, enabling automatic failover and preserving availability for writes. Cross-region read replicas in `us-east1` and `us-west1` place read capacity nearer to applications in those regions, which improves read latency while the HA primary handles writes in its configured region.

**Learn more:** [About high availability | Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/high-availability) · [About replication in Cloud SQL | Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/replication)","trackingInfo":{"questionId":"cd248e5c-1d49-45c8-b47a-ad9565cfcd63","examProvider":"google","examName":"professional-cloud-database-engineer","mode":"default"}}]]

",["$","$L55",null,{"choices":{"A":"Use Cloud Spanner with a customer-managed encryption key (CMEK).","B":"Use Cloud Spanner with default encryption.","C":"Use Cloud SQL with a customer-managed encryption key (CMEK).","D":"Use Bigtable with default encryption."},"correctAnswer":"A","explanation":"Cloud Spanner multi-region configurations replicate data across regions and maintain availability during regional failures. Spanner supports customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) in Cloud KMS, which lets the customer control key location, lifecycle, permissions, and rotation. Cloud KMS symmetric encryption keys use AES-256.

**Learn more:** [Regional, dual-region, and multi-region configurations | Spanner](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/instance-configurations) · [Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) overview | Spanner](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/cmek)","trackingInfo":{"questionId":"d8596376-cab1-43ef-8438-43640725c3c6","examProvider":"google","examName":"professional-cloud-database-engineer","mode":"default"}}]]

",["$","$L55",null,{"choices":{"A":"Use Ora2pg for schema and code conversion and data migration.","B":"Use Ora2pg for schema and code conversion. Use the oracle_fdw extension in AlloyDB and replicate data from source to destination by using CREATE TABLE AS SELECT statements.","C":"Use Database Migration Service. Set up a conversion workspace for schema and code conversion. Create a migration job to perform backfill and change data capture to replicate data from source to destination.","D":"Use Database Migration Service. Set up a legacy conversion workspace for schema and code conversion. Create a migration job to perform backfill and change data capture to replicate data from source to destination."},"correctAnswer":"C","explanation":"Database Migration Service conversion workspaces convert Oracle schema and supported code objects, including stored procedures, to PostgreSQL syntax. Legacy conversion workspaces are older, more limited, use Ora2Pg-based conversion, and are not recommended for migrations.

**Learn more:** [Conversion workspaces | Database Migration Service for heterogeneous Oracle to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/oracle-to-alloydb/about-conversion-workspaces) · [Create a migration job | Database Migration Service for heterogeneous Oracle to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/oracle-to-alloydb/create-migration-job)","trackingInfo":{"questionId":"0946b622-2fd9-4a93-838a-57e2096b3f2f","examProvider":"google","examName":"professional-cloud-database-engineer","mode":"default"}}]]
Your company is adopting AlloyDB for a business-critical application with these requirements:  
  
- RTO: Under 4 hours  
- RPO: 6 hours (maximum tolerated data loss)  
- Daily backups with a 7-day retention period  
  
You must design a solution that meets these requirements.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Make a daily backup and store on Cloud Storage.
Set a longer retention period for automatic backups.
Disable automatic backups and manually export data to Cloud Storage.
Configure automatic backups and enable continuous backup and recovery.

questions.explanation:
AlloyDB automated backups can be scheduled daily and retained for seven days. Enabling continuous backup and recovery provides point-in-time recovery and an RPO of zero, which is more stringent than a maximum six-hour data-loss tolerance; it also supports recovery from a recent point in time for the required recovery objective.

**Learn more:** [Data backup and recovery overview | AlloyDB for PostgreSQL](https://cloud.google.com/alloydb/docs/backup/overview) · [Configure backup plans | AlloyDB for PostgreSQL](https://cloud.google.com/alloydb/docs/backup/configure)

You use Memorystore for Redis to cache frequently accessed data and enhance your application's performance. Recently, the application has experienced sudden latency spikes while interacting with the Memorystore for Redis instance. After reviewing the logs, you find a large number of "evicted keys" messages. You want to reduce both the frequency of latency spikes and their effect on the application. What should you do?

options.text: Increase the time to live (TTL) value of all the keys within the cache.
Redeploy your application to the same zone as the Memorystore instance.
Scale the Memorystore instance to a larger memory size.
Enable read replicas. Deploy additional read replica instances to distribute read workloads.

questions.explanation:
Evicted keys indicate that the instance has reached its `maxmemory` limit. Evictions can remove frequently used cached data and degrade application performance; increasing the instance’s memory capacity reduces memory pressure and lowers eviction frequency. Google Cloud recommends scaling up when cache capacity is insufficient for the workload.

**Learn more:** [Memory management best practices | Memorystore for Redis](https://docs.cloud.google.com/memorystore/docs/redis/memory-management-best-practices) · [Supported monitoring metrics | Memorystore for Redis](https://docs.cloud.google.com/memorystore/docs/redis/supported-monitoring-metrics)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You released a popular mobile game and use a 50 TB Cloud Spanner instance to store game data in a PITR-enabled production environment. After analyzing game statistics, you discover that some players are exploiting a loophole to collect extra points and reach the leaderboard. Another DBA accidentally executed an emergency bug-fix script that corrupted some production data. You need to assess the extent of the data corruption and restore the production environment. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: If the corruption is significant, use backup and restore, and specify a recovery timestamp.
If the corruption is significant, perform a stale read and specify a recovery timestamp. Write the results back.
If the corruption is significant, use import and export.
If the corruption is insignificant, use backup and restore, and specify a recovery timestamp.
If the corruption is insignificant, perform a stale read and specify a recovery timestamp. Write the results back.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Spanner PITR uses stale reads at a timestamp before corruption to surgically recover a portion of a database, after which the recovered results are written back. For significant or whole-database corruption, create a backup at the required recovery timestamp and restore it to a new database. Backup and restore is the appropriate full-database recovery method rather than export/import for this scenario.

**Learn more:** [Point-in-time recovery (PITR) overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/pitr) · [Recover data using point-in-time recovery (PITR)](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/use-pitr?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a Cloud SQL for MySQL Enterprise instance with four read replicas. Your next scheduled maintenance event is set for tomorrow at 6 PM. Your security team identifies an important security vulnerability. At 8 PM today, management notifies you to update the primary instance and all four read replicas during approved business downtime today at 11 PM. What should you do?

options.text: Reschedule the upcoming scheduled maintenance to happen today at 11 PM.
Perform self-service maintenance on the selected read replicas.
Perform self-service maintenance on the primary instance during scheduled business downtime.
Reschedule the upcoming scheduled maintenance of the primary instance to apply updates immediately.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL self-service maintenance is intended when an update is needed before the next scheduled maintenance event. When it is initiated on a primary instance with read replicas, Cloud SQL applies the target maintenance version to all read replicas and then updates the primary instance. Scheduled maintenance cannot be rescheduled when less than 24 hours remain before its originally scheduled time.

**Learn more:** [Perform self-service maintenance — Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/self-service-maintenance) · [Maintenance updates on Cloud SQL instances — Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/maintenance)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your digital-native business operates its database workloads on Cloud SQL. Your website must remain globally accessible 24/7. You need to ready your Cloud SQL instance for high availability (HA) and want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Set up manual backups.
Create a PostgreSQL database on-premises as the HA option.
Configure single zone availability for automated backups.
Enable point-in-time recovery.
Schedule automated backups.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL high-availability instances require automated backups and point-in-time recovery (PITR) to be enabled. Automated backups provide scheduled recoverable backup points, while PITR supports recovery to a selected point using transaction logs.

**Learn more:** [About high availability — Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/high-availability?hl=en) · [Configure point-in-time recovery — Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/backup-recovery/configure-pitr)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are setting up a new Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL database instance in Google Cloud. Your application team wants to deploy one primary instance, one standby instance, and one read replica instance. You must ensure that you follow Google-recommended practices for high availability. What should you do?

options.text: Configure the primary instance in zone A, the standby instance in zone C, and the read replica in zone B, all in the same region.
Configure the primary and standby instances in zone A and the read replica in zone B, all in the same region.
Configure the primary instance in one region, the standby instance in a second region, and the read replica in a third region.
Configure the primary, standby, and read replica instances in zone A, all in the same region.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud SQL high-availability configuration uses a primary and standby in separate zones within the same region. Google recommends placing read replicas in a different zone from both the primary and standby so that the replica can continue operating if either of those zones has an outage.

**Learn more:** [About high availability | Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/high-availability) · [About replication in Cloud SQL | Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/replication)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company is launching a gaming application that uses a Firestore database. You need to determine an easy-to-manage, cost-effective solution for automating the schedule of Firestore data exports. What should you do?

options.text: Create a new Compute Engine, and set up a cron Job to run the gcloud firestore export command.
Use Dataflow to create a custom pipeline to extract data from Firestore, transform it into the desired format, and load it into a Cloud Storage bucket at regular intervals.
Use Cloud Scheduler to trigger a Cloud Function that executes the Firestore export process.
Use the Firebase Admin SDK to programmatically schedule and manage exports.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Scheduler can run on a defined schedule and invoke a Cloud Function that initiates Firestore’s managed export operation. This serverless pattern is the documented approach for scheduled Firestore exports and avoids operating a virtual machine or building an unnecessary data-processing pipeline.

**Learn more:** [Schedule data exports — Firestore in Native mode](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firestore/native/docs/solutions/schedule-export) · [Schedule data exports — Cloud Scheduler](https://docs.cloud.google.com/scheduler/docs/firestore-data-exports?hl=en)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: Your company is closing its on-premises data center and migrating Oracle databases that use Oracle Real Application Clusters (RAC) to Google Cloud. You want to make minimal or no application changes during the database migration. What should you do?

options.text: Migrate the Oracle databases to Cloud Spanner.
Migrate the Oracle databases to Compute Engine.
Migrate the Oracle databases to Cloud SQL.
Migrate the Oracle databases to Bare Metal Solution for Oracle.

questions.explanation:
Bare Metal Solution for Oracle lets organizations run Oracle databases, including Oracle Real Application Clusters (RAC), on certified bare-metal infrastructure while retaining existing Oracle capabilities, tools, and operational practices. This supports a lift-and-shift migration with minimal application changes.\
\
**Learn more:** [Bare Metal Solution for Oracle](https://cloud.google.com/bare-metal)

questions.question: Your company is closing its on-premises data center and migrating Oracle databases that use Oracle Real Application Clusters (RAC) to Google Cloud. You want to make minimal or no application changes during the database migration. What should you do?

options.text: Set Terraform deletion_protection to true.
Rerun terraform apply.
Create a read replica.
Use point-in-time-recovery (PITR) to recover the database.

questions.explanation:
For a Cloud SQL instance managed by Terraform, `deletion_protection = true` is a Terraform-level safeguard that prevents Terraform from deleting the instance. If a plan requires a destroy-and-recreate operation, Terraform blocks it until deletion protection is explicitly disabled.

**Learn more:** [Prevent deletion of a Cloud SQL instance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/deletion-protection?hl=en) · [Upgrade the database major version in-place](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/upgrade-major-db-version-inplace)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization runs a critical production database on a Compute Engine virtual machine (VM). The VM uses an ext4-formatted persistent disk for its data files. The database will soon exhaust its available storage. You need to implement a solution that prevents downtime. What should you do?

options.text: In the Google Cloud Console, increase the size of the persistent disk, and use the resize2fs command to extend the disk.
In the Google Cloud Console, increase the size of the persistent disk, and use the fdisk command to verify that the new space is ready to use
In the Google Cloud Console, create a snapshot of the persistent disk, restore the snapshot to a new larger disk, unmount the old disk, mount the new disk, and restart the database service.
In the Google Cloud Console, create a new persistent disk attached to the VM, and configure the database service to move the files to the new disk.

questions.explanation:
A Persistent Disk can be increased while attached to a running VM. For an ext4-formatted non-boot data disk, run `resize2fs` after increasing the disk size so the filesystem uses the added capacity; the VM does not need to be restarted.

**Learn more:** [Modify the size of a Persistent Disk](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/disks/resize-persistent-disk)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A retail company currently uses DynamoDB to store product-catalog data. Because data volumes are increasing and the company needs improved scalability, cost efficiency, and AI features, it has decided to migrate its data to Bigtable.  
  
You need a cost-effective migration with minimal downtime and effort while maintaining data consistency between the two databases. What should you do?

options.text: Export the DynamoDB data to CSV files, upload them to Cloud Storage, and use the cbt CLI to import the data into Bigtable.
Create a Dataflow pipeline using the DynamoDBIO and BigtableIO connectors to stream data from DynamoDB to Bigtable in near real time.
Develop a custom script using the DynamoDB and Bigtable APIs to directly transfer data between the two databases.
Use Dataproc to export the data from DynamoDB and load it into Bigtable.

questions.explanation:
A Dataflow pipeline using DynamoDBIO and BigtableIO provides managed, scalable data movement from DynamoDB to Bigtable. Streaming records in near real time keeps the target closely synchronized during migration, which supports a short cutover window and avoids the operational effort and consistency gap of a one-time file export or a custom transfer program. BigtableIO supports batch and streaming pipeline operations with Dataflow.

**Learn more:** [Bigtable Beam connector](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/beam-connector) · [Migrate from DynamoDB to Bigtable](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/dynamodb-users)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company runs a critical application on-premises using PostgreSQL. The application needs minimal downtime during migration and must tolerate regional outages. You are evaluating a Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus edition instance running PostgreSQL. You need to ensure the migration meets these requirements with minimal effort.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use the PostgreSQL interface for Spanner.
Configure cross-region replicas, and test failover.
Select standard storage options, and conduct regular database backups.
Focus on provisioning large compute instances for optimal performance during failover.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL cross-region replicas support planned regional migration with minimal downtime by allowing replication to catch up before promotion. In Enterprise Plus, a cross-region replica can be designated for advanced disaster recovery and failed over during a regional failure; failover testing validates that recovery capability.

**Learn more:** [Promote replicas for regional migration or disaster recovery](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/replication/cross-region-replicas) · [Use advanced disaster recovery (DR)](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/use-advanced-disaster-recovery)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company runs a globally available, mission-critical inventory-management system on Cloud Spanner. After loading stock keeping unit (SKU) and product-catalog data from a company acquisition, you observed hotspots in the Cloud Spanner database. You want to apply Google-recommended schema-design practices to prevent performance degradation. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use an auto-incrementing value as the primary key.
Normalize the data model.
Promote low-cardinality attributes in multi-attribute primary keys.
Promote high-cardinality attributes in multi-attribute primary keys.
Use bit-reverse sequential value as the primary key.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Spanner distributes data and write load by primary-key ranges. Putting a high-cardinality attribute first in a composite primary key helps distribute writes across more key ranges, whereas a low-cardinality leading attribute can concentrate them. Bit-reversed sequential primary-key values are distributed evenly across the key space, avoiding the hotspot behavior caused by monotonic auto-incrementing values.

**Learn more:** [Schema design best practices | Spanner](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/schema-design?hl=en) · [Primary key default values management | Spanner](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/primary-key-default-value)

questions.question: Your company is building a new global transactional application that must be ACID compliant and provide 99.999% availability. You are responsible for choosing the appropriate Google Cloud database to act as the datastore for this new application. What should you do?

options.text: Use Firestore.
Use Cloud Spanner.
Use Cloud SQL.
Use Bigtable.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Spanner provides ACID read-write transactions for globally distributed transactional applications. Its multi-regional and dual-regional configurations have a 99.999% monthly uptime objective, satisfying the required availability level.\
\
**Learn more:** [Transactions overview — Spanner](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/transactions?hl=en) · [Cloud Spanner Service Level Agreement](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/sla)

questions.question: Your company is building a new global transactional application that must be ACID compliant and provide 99.999% availability. You are responsible for choosing the appropriate Google Cloud database to act as the datastore for this new application. What should you do?

options.text: Use linear scaling to implement the Autoscaler-based architecture
Use direct scaling to implement the Autoscaler-based architecture.
Upgrade the Cloud Spanner instance on a periodic basis during the scheduled maintenance window.
Set up alerts that are triggered when Cloud Spanner utilization metrics breach the threshold, and then schedule an upgrade during the scheduled maintenance window.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Spanner Autoscaler's linear scaling method is designed for workloads that change gradually or experience a few large peaks. It automatically calculates and adds the compute capacity required to keep utilization below the configured threshold, supporting continued growth and holiday concurrency spikes.

**Learn more:** [Autoscaler tool overview | Spanner | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/autoscaler-tool-overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization has a security policy requiring that every Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL database be secure. You want to safeguard sensitive data with a key that satisfies particular locality or residency requirements. Your organization must control the key's lifecycle activities. You must ensure that data is encrypted at rest and in transit. What should you do?

options.text: Create the database with Google-managed encryption keys.
Create the database with customer-managed encryption keys.
Create the database persistent disk with Google-managed encryption keys.
Create the database persistent disk with customer-managed encryption keys.

questions.explanation:
Customer-managed encryption keys let an organization manage encryption-key lifecycle activities in Cloud KMS and use keys located in the required region. Cloud SQL supports CMEK when creating the database instance, while encryption at rest and in transit is provided by the service.

**Learn more:** [Use customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) — Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/configure-cmek?hl=en) · [Data residency overview — Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/data-residency-overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are migrating a critical production database from Amazon RDS for MySQL to Cloud SQL for MySQL using Google Cloud's Database Migration Service. You want to minimize disruption to the production database while also optimizing migration performance. What should you do?

options.text: Create and start multiple Database Migration Service jobs to migrate your database to the target Cloud SQL for MySQL instance.
Upgrade the Amazon RDS for MySQL primary instance to an instance with more vCPUs and memory, and then run Google Cloud's Database Migration Service.
Create a single Database Migration Service migration job with initial load parallelism configured to maximum on the source Amazon RDS for MySQL read replica.
Create a single Database Migration Service migration job with initial Load Parallelism configured to Maximum on the Amazon RDS for MySQL primary instance.

questions.explanation:
Data dump parallelism accelerates the initial migration load, but it increases load on the source database. Using an Amazon RDS MySQL read replica as the migration source isolates that work from the production primary, and setting Initial Load Parallelism to Maximum maximizes initial-load throughput. Google Cloud also documents using a read replica when locking or disrupting the source is not acceptable.

**Learn more:** [Known limitations — Database Migration Service for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/mysql/known-limitations) · [Migrating from Amazon RDS MySQL without SUPERUSER privileges](https://docs.cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/mysql/rds-no-superuser)

questions.question: Your organization operates a ticketing system that requires an online marketing analytics and reporting application. You need to choose a relational database that can manage hundreds of terabytes of data to support this new application. Which database should you use?

options.text: Cloud SQL
BigQuery
Cloud Spanner
Bigtable

questions.explanation:
Cloud Spanner is a fully managed, horizontally scalable relational database that provides SQL semantics and transactional consistency at global scale, making it suitable for an application that requires relational data management at hundreds-of-terabytes scale.\
\
**Learn more:** [Spanner documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs) · [Spanner: Always-on, virtually unlimited scale database](https://cloud.google.com/spanner)

questions.question: Your organization runs a Firestore-backed Firebase app that delivers the same top ten news stories each day to a large worldwide audience. You want to optimize content delivery while reducing cost and latency. What should you do?

options.text: Enable serializable isolation in the Firebase app.
Deploy a US multi-region Firestore location.
Build a Firestore bundle, and deploy bundles to Cloud CDN.
Create a Firestore index on the news story date.

questions.explanation:
Firestore bundles can package the daily news data for download and client-side loading. Serving those bundles through a CDN caches and replicates the static content close to users globally, reducing repeated Firestore reads, delivery cost, and latency.\
\
**Learn more:** [Using the Firestore Bundle Builder Extension](https://firebase.google.com/docs/extensions/official/firestore-bundle-builder?hl=en)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: Your organization runs a Firestore-backed Firebase app that delivers the same top ten news stories each day to a large worldwide audience. You want to optimize content delivery while reducing cost and latency. What should you do?

options.text: Use the default app profile with single-cluster routing.
Use the default app profile with multi-cluster routing.
Create a custom app profile with multi-cluster routing.
Create a custom app profile with single-cluster routing.

questions.explanation:
A custom app profile using multi-cluster routing routes traffic to an available cluster in the replicated Bigtable instance. When one cluster becomes unavailable, Bigtable automatically fails over requests to another available cluster. Single-cluster routing cannot provide that automatic cluster failover.

**Learn more:** [Manage failovers | Bigtable](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/managing-failovers) · [Create and configure app profiles | Bigtable](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/configuring-app-profiles)

options.text: Set up a Shared VPC, configure multiple service projects, and create firewall rules.
Set up Serverless VPC Access.
Set up Private Service Connect.
Set up Traffic Director.

questions.explanation:
A Shared VPC provides a common VPC network for Compute Engine resources in multiple service projects. For Bare Metal Solution, create the VLAN attachments in the Shared VPC host project so resources attached to that VPC can reach the Bare Metal Solution servers, and use firewall rules to restrict traffic to only the required database communication.

**Learn more:** [Provide security for enterprise workloads in a Bare Metal Solution environment](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bare-metal/docs/bms-security) · [Deploy your Bare Metal Solution environment](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bare-metal/docs/bms-deploy)

You manage a meeting-booking application that uses Cloud SQL. During an important launch, the Cloud SQL instance underwent a maintenance event that caused more than 5 minutes of downtime and negatively affected your production application. You need to promptly address the maintenance issue to avoid unplanned events in the future. What should you do?

options.text: Set your production instance's maintenance window to non-business hours.
Migrate the Cloud SQL instance to Cloud Spanner to avoid any future disruptions due to maintenance.
Contact Support to understand why your Cloud SQL instance had a downtime of more than 5 minutes.
Use Cloud Scheduler to schedule a maintenance window of no longer than 5 minutes.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL maintenance can require an instance restart and downtime. Configuring a maintenance window during non-business hours lets Cloud SQL schedule eligible maintenance when brief disruption has the least effect on the production application.

**Learn more:** [Cloud SQL overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/introduction) · [Maintenance updates on Cloud SQL instances](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/maintenance)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company plans to migrate an Oracle-based application to Google Cloud. The application team currently uses Oracle Recovery Manager (RMAN) to back up the database to tape for long-term retention (LTR). You need a cost-effective backup and restore solution that satisfies a 2-hour recovery time objective (RTO) and a 15-minute recovery point objective (RPO). What should you do?

options.text: Migrate the Oracle databases to Bare Metal Solution for Oracle, and store backups on tapes on-premises.
Migrate the Oracle databases to Bare Metal Solution for Oracle, and use Actifio to store backup files on Cloud Storage using the Nearline Storage class.
Migrate the Oracle databases to Bare Metal Solution for Oracle, and back up the Oracle databases to Cloud Storage using the Standard Storage class.
Migrate the Oracle databases to Compute Engine, and store backups on tapes on-premises.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Backup and DR (formerly Actifio) supports application-consistent, incremental-forever backups for Oracle databases on Bare Metal Solution and enables rapid recovery by making database images available without a full traditional restore. Its Cloud Storage-backed long-term retention can use the lower-cost Nearline class, while backup scheduling and recovery capabilities can meet a 15-minute RPO and 2-hour RTO. Bare Metal Solution also preserves Oracle compatibility and existing operational practices.

**Learn more:** [Disaster recovery options for Oracle database workloads](https://cloud.google.com/bare-metal/docs/oracle-db-dr-options) · [Solution Guide: Google Cloud Backup and DR for Oracle on Bare Metal Solution](https://cloud.google.com/bare-metal/docs/solutions/oracle/bms-oracle-backup-and-dr)

questions.domain: Design scalable and highly available cloud database solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your ecommerce website collects user clickstream data to analyze customer traffic patterns in real time and enable personalization features on the website. You plan to analyze this data with big-data tools. You need a low-latency solution that can store 8 TB of data and scale to millions of read and write requests per second. What should you do?

options.text: Write your data into Bigtable and use Dataproc and the Apache Hbase libraries for analysis.
Deploy a Cloud SQL environment with read replicas for improved performance. Use Datastream to export data to Cloud Storage and analyze with Dataproc and the Cloud Storage connector.
Use Memorystore to handle your low-latency requirements and for real-time analytics.
Stream your data into BigQuery and use Dataproc and the BigQuery Storage API to analyze large volumes of data.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Bigtable is a low-latency, wide-column NoSQL database for large single-keyed datasets, high read/write throughput, and horizontal scaling. It can store terabytes to petabytes, supports the Apache HBase client libraries, and integrates with Dataproc, so it fits clickstream storage, real-time personalization, and big-data analysis.

**Learn more:** [Bigtable overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/overview) · [Dataproc optional HBase component](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dataproc/docs/concepts/components/hbase)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company plans to migrate its 5 TB on-premises MySQL database to Cloud SQL for MySQL. You need a Google-recommended method for schema and data migration. Downtime must be kept to a minimum while continuous data replication is maintained.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use Dataflow to set up a custom ETL pipeline to extract data from the on-premises database, and load the data into Cloud SQL.
Use Database Migration Service to migrate data from the on-premises database to Cloud SQL, then promote the Cloud SQL instance as the primary after migration is complete.
Use the mysqldump utility to create a backup of the on-premises database, and restore that backup into a new Cloud SQL instance.
Manually export the data from the on-premises database CSV format, and import this data into a new Cloud SQL instance.

questions.explanation:
Database Migration Service supports continuous migrations from self-managed on-premises MySQL to Cloud SQL for MySQL. It migrates the initial schema and data, continuously replicates subsequent changes, and promotes the Cloud SQL destination to a primary instance for cutover with minimal downtime.

**Learn more:** [Types of migration | Database Migration Service for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/mysql/migration-types) · [Migrate a database to Cloud SQL for MySQL by using Database Migration Service](https://docs.cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/mysql/quickstart)

Your organization has deployed a new version of a critical application that uses Cloud SQL for MySQL with high availability (HA) and binary logging enabled to store transactional information. The most recent application release contained an error that caused extensive data corruption in your Cloud SQL for MySQL database. You need to minimize data loss. What should you do?

options.text: Open the Google Cloud Console, navigate to SQL > Backups, and select the last version of the automated backup before the corruption.
Reload the Cloud SQL for MySQL database using the LOAD DATA command to load data from CSV files that were used to initialize the instance.
Perform a point-in-time recovery of your Cloud SQL for MySQL database, selecting a date and time before the data was corrupted.
Fail over to the Cloud SQL for MySQL HA instance. Use that instance to recover the transactions that occurred before the corruption.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL for MySQL point-in-time recovery restores an instance to a specific time by using a backup and the continuous binary logs retained since that backup. Selecting a recovery time immediately before the corruption minimizes lost valid transactions. High-availability failover protects against infrastructure failure, but the standby reflects logical data corruption.

**Learn more:** [Perform point-in-time recovery (PITR) — Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/backup-recovery/pitr?hl=en) · [About high availability — Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/high-availability?hl=en)

The company’s user base across North America is growing rapidly, nearly doubling over the past 6 months. This growth is substantially increasing query volume on the mission-critical Cloud SQL database, resulting in noticeable performance problems and slower query response times. You suspect that the Cloud SQL instance might be unable to handle the additional load. You need to determine the root cause of this performance bottleneck and ensure that the database can scale with the expanding user base. What should you do?

options.text: Migrate the database to Spanner.
Evaluate the application connection pooling configuration settings.
Review Cloud SQL System Insights for the instance, and analyze CPU, memory, and storage utilization metrics.
Create two Cloud SQL instances, and split the workload between them.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL System Insights provides instance health and performance data, including CPU utilization, memory usage, disk utilization, and metric charts for analyzing latency and throughput. Reviewing these metrics identifies whether resource saturation is causing the bottleneck and supplies the evidence needed to select an appropriate scaling action.

**Learn more:** [Use system insights to improve system performance | Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/use-system-insights?hl=en)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have several on-premises Percona Server for MySQL 8.0 instances supporting mission-critical applications. The workload is read-heavy, with 80%+ reads, and every instance contains several TBs of data. You want to migrate to Google Cloud with minimal downtime and as few changes as possible.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use Database Migration Service to migrate to Alloy DB.
Use Datastream to migrate to Cloud SQL Enterprise
Use the spanner-migration-tool to migrate to Spanner.
Use Database Migration Service to migrate to Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus.

questions.explanation:
Database Migration Service supports homogeneous migrations from self-managed MySQL 8.0 sources to Cloud SQL for MySQL and can perform an initial load followed by continuous replication, minimizing cutover downtime. Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus is designed for demanding, mission-critical MySQL workloads and retains MySQL compatibility, avoiding the greater database and application changes associated with Spanner or an AlloyDB migration.

**Learn more:** [Supported source and destination databases | Database Migration Service](https://docs.cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/supported-databases) · [Database Migration Service documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your rapidly expanding ecommerce company is migrating its analytics workloads to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL. You expect reporting-query volume to increase significantly as the business grows. You need a read-pool strategy that scales analytics operations for anticipated future growth while minimizing costs. What should you do?

options.text: Direct all complex, long-running analytics queries to the primary instance, and only use read pools for short, frequent reports.
Change the instance sizes of the read nodes in the read pool.
Begin with minimal read pools and iteratively expand or shrink them based on real-time load monitoring to optimize resource allocation.
Assign all reporting queries to a single, large read pool to maximize the combined compute resources available for analytics.

questions.explanation:
AlloyDB read pool instances provide read-only workload scaling and support changing the number of nodes manually or automatically in response to real-time resource usage. Beginning with a small pool and expanding or shrinking it as observed demand changes matches capacity to the reporting workload and helps control compute costs.

**Learn more:** [Scale an instance | AlloyDB for PostgreSQL](https://cloud.google.com/alloydb/docs/instance-read-pool-scale) · [AlloyDB overview](https://cloud.google.com/alloydb/docs/overview)

questions.domain: Design scalable and highly available cloud database solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization operates a high-volume, low-latency application on Bigtable. You must lower costs without sacrificing performance. What should you do?

options.text: Reduce replication factor across clusters.
Consolidate multiple small clusters into a single large cluster.
Analyze application access patterns to strategically redesign the schema and adjust the node count.
Switch to a lower-performance storage type for all clusters.

questions.explanation:
Bigtable node capacity is a primary cost driver, and effective schema design depends on the application’s access patterns. Analyzing those patterns can identify inefficient distribution or hotspots, allowing the schema and node count to be right-sized while preserving the throughput and latency required by the workload.

**Learn more:** [Design a schema | Bigtable | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/schema-design-steps) · [Scaling | Bigtable | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/scaling)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You deployed a Cloud SQL for SQL Server instance and also created a cross-region read replica for disaster recovery (DR). Your company requires maintaining and monitoring a recovery point objective (RPO) of less than 5 minutes. You need to confirm that the cross-region read replica meets the permitted RPO. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud SQL instance monitoring.
Use the Cloud Monitoring dashboard with available metrics from Cloud SQL.
Use Cloud SQL logs.
Use the SQL Server Always On Availability Group dashboard.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL for SQL Server read replicas use SQL Server Always On Availability Groups with asynchronous replication. The SQL Server Always On Availability Group dashboard provides the replica replication status and failover-related data-loss information needed to assess whether the replica’s recovery point falls within the required five-minute RPO. Google Cloud’s cross-region replica DR guidance specifically identifies this dashboard in SQL Server Management Studio for checking replica replication status.

**Learn more:** [Promote replicas for regional migration or disaster recovery — Cloud SQL for SQL Server](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/sqlserver/replication/cross-region-replicas)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are migrating a 2 TB on-premises PostgreSQL cluster to Compute Engine. You want to configure the new environment on an Ubuntu virtual machine instance in Google Cloud and seed data to a new instance. You need to plan the database migration to ensure minimal downtime. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Take a full export while the database is offline.2. Create a bucket in Cloud Storage.3. Transfer the dump file to the bucket you just created.4. Import the dump file into the Google Cloud primary server.B.1. Take a full export while the database is offline.2. Create a bucket in Cloud Storage.3. Transfer the dump file to the bucket you just created.4. Restore the backup into the Google Cloud primary server.

1. Take a full backup while the database is online.2. Create a bucket in Cloud Storage.3. Transfer the backup to the bucket you just created.4. Restore the backup into the Google Cloud primary server.5. Create a recovery.conf file in the $PG_DATA directory.6. Stop the source database.7. Transfer the write ahead logs to the bucket you created before.8. Start the PostgreSQL service.9. Wait until Google Cloud primary server syncs with the running primary server.

1. Take a full export while the database is online.2. Create a bucket in Cloud Storage.3. Transfer the dump file and write-ahead logs to the bucket you just created.4. Restore the dump file into the Google Cloud primary server.5. Create a recovery.conf file in the $PG_DATA directory.6. Stop the source database.7. Transfer the write-ahead logs to the bucket you created before.8. Start the PostgreSQL service.9. Wait until the Google Cloud primary server syncs with the running primary server.

questions.explanation:
A PostgreSQL physical base backup can be taken while the source remains online. Restoring that backup at the destination and applying archived WAL lets the destination continuously recover changes made after the backup. Stopping source writes only for the final WAL transfer and waiting for replay to catch up limits the outage to the cutover period. Logical exports do not provide the physical data files needed for WAL recovery.

**Learn more:** [PostgreSQL: Continuous Archiving and Point-in-Time Recovery](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/continuous-archiving.html) · [PostgreSQL: Log-Shipping Standby Servers](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/warm-standby.html)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: You need to migrate a 1 TB PostgreSQL database from a Compute Engine VM to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL while ensuring minimal downtime. What should you do?

options.text: Export the data from the existing database, and load the data into a new Cloud SQL database.
Use Migrate for Compute Engine to complete the migration.
Use Datastream to complete the migration.
Use Database Migration Service to complete the migration.

questions.explanation:
Database Migration Service is designed for PostgreSQL migrations to Cloud SQL. It performs an initial data load and continuously replicates subsequent changes, allowing cutover when the destination is synchronized and thereby minimizing downtime.\
\
**Learn more:** [Database Migration Service overview](https://cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/overview) · [Database Migration Service](https://cloud.google.com/database-migration)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: You need to migrate a 1 TB PostgreSQL database from a Compute Engine VM to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL while ensuring minimal downtime. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Create your instance with a specified external (public) IP address.2. Choose the VPC and create firewall rules to allow only connections from Cloud Run into your instance.3. Use Cloud SQL Auth proxy to connect to the instance.

1. Create your instance with a specified external (public) IP address.2. Choose the VPC and create firewall rules to allow only connections from Cloud Run into your instance.3. Connect to the instance using a connection pool to best manage connections to the instance.

1. Create your instance with a specified internal (private) IP address.2. Choose the VPC with private service connection configured.3. Configure the Serverless VPC Access connector in the same VPC network as your Cloud SQL instance.4. Use Cloud SQL Auth proxy to connect to the instance.

1. Create your instance with a specified internal (private) IP address.2. Choose the VPC with private service connection configured.3. Configure the Serverless VPC Access connector in the same VPC network as your Cloud SQL instance.4. Connect to the instance using a connection pool to best manage connections to the instance.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL private IP requires private services access for the selected VPC. Cloud Run can reach the private IP through a Serverless VPC Access connector in that VPC, without exposing a public database endpoint. For this private-IP route, Cloud Run connects directly to Cloud SQL; using a connection pool helps control the number of database connections created by scalable Cloud Run instances.

**Learn more:** [Connect from Cloud Run | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/connect-run) · [Learn about using private IP | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/private-ip)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A customer runs an on-premises MySQL database with read replicas. Its nightly incremental backups are costly and create maintenance overhead. You want to follow Google-recommended practices to migrate the database to Google Cloud while ensuring minimal downtime. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster, install MySQL on the cluster, and then import the dump file.
Use the mysqldump utility to take a backup of the existing on-premises database, and then import it into Cloud SQL.
Create a Compute Engine VM, install MySQL on the VM, and then import the dump file.
Create an external replica, and use Cloud SQL to synchronize the data to the replica.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL can replicate from an external MySQL source, continuously applying source changes to a Cloud SQL replica. After the replica catches up, it can be promoted for cutover, which supports migration with minimal downtime while moving database administration to the managed Cloud SQL service.

**Learn more:** [About replicating from an external server | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/replication/external-server) · [Configure Cloud SQL and the external server for replication | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/replication/configure-replication-from-external)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building a Python application that will use AlloyDB for PostgreSQL as its backend datastore. Your organization’s security requirements prohibit using usernames and passwords for database authentication. How should you build the application?

options.text: Use any PostgreSQL-compatible Python client. Connect to the AlloyDB cluster by using Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP).
Use the AlloyDB Python connector. Use automated IAM authentication for connectivity.
Use the AlloyDB Python connector. Enforce SSL connectivity to AlloyDB by using the gcloud alloydb instance update command with the --ssl-mode=ENCRYPTED_ONLY option.
Use any PostgreSQL-compatible Python client. Use a service account name and credential as the username and password respectively during connection.

questions.explanation:
The AlloyDB Python connector supports automatic IAM database authentication, which uses the IAM principal running the application and manages short-lived access tokens on the application's behalf instead of requiring a database password. IAM authentication is the appropriate passwordless database-authentication method for AlloyDB.

**Learn more:** [Connect using the AlloyDB Language Connectors](https://docs.cloud.google.com/alloydb/docs/connect-language-connectors?hl=en) · [AlloyDB for PostgreSQL IAM database authentication](https://docs.cloud.google.com/alloydb/docs/database-users/iam-authentication)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A MySQL database is currently running on Cloud SQL, with a read replica in a separate zone for non-mission-critical analytics workloads. You want to provide high availability (HA) for the analytics workloads while keeping costs low. What should you do?

options.text: Increase the size of the read replica instance and enable HA.
Enable HA on the current read replica.
Create a new HA instance in the same zone as the primary.
Create a new HA instance in a different region than the primary.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL for MySQL supports enabling HA on read replicas. Configuring the existing analytics read replica for regional HA provides failover across zones while avoiding the cost of provisioning an additional HA instance.

**Learn more:** [About high availability | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/high-availability) · [Enable and disable high availability | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/configure-ha)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],During an internal audit, you discover that one of your Cloud SQL for MySQL instances does not have high availability (HA) enabled. You want to follow Google-recommended practices to enable HA on the existing instance. What should you do?

options.text: Create a new Cloud SQL for MySQL instance, enable HA, and use the export and import option to migrate your data.
Create a new Cloud SQL for MySQL instance, enable HA, and use Cloud Data Fusion to migrate your data.
Use the gcloud instances patch command to update your existing Cloud SQL for MySQL instance.
Shut down your existing Cloud SQL for MySQL instance, and enable HA.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL for MySQL can be converted from a zonal instance to a regional, highly available instance in place. Google documents using `gcloud sql instances patch` to set the availability type to `REGIONAL`; high availability also requires automated backups and binary logging. The reconfiguration restarts the instance, but it does not require creating and migrating to a new instance.

**Learn more:** [Enable and disable high availability — Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/configure-ha?hl=en)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: You are troubleshooting a connection problem with a newly deployed Cloud SQL instance on Google Cloud. While reviewing the Cloud SQL Proxy logs, you find the message `Error 403: Access Not Configured`. What should you do?

options.text: Check the app.yaml value cloud_sql_instances for a misspelled or incorrect instance connection name.
Check whether your service account has cloudsql.instances.connect permission.
Enable the Cloud SQL Admin API.
Ensure that you are using an external (public) IP address interface.

questions.explanation:
The Cloud SQL Auth Proxy requires the Cloud SQL Admin API. When that API is disabled, the proxy logs `Error 403: Access Not Configured`; enabling the Cloud SQL Admin API resolves this specific error.\
\
**Learn more:** [Connect using the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/connect-auth-proxy?hl=en)

questions.domain: Design scalable and highly available cloud database solutions
questions.question: You are troubleshooting a connection problem with a newly deployed Cloud SQL instance on Google Cloud. While reviewing the Cloud SQL Proxy logs, you find the message `Error 403: Access Not Configured`. What should you do?

options.text: Scale up the Bigtable instance by manually adding more nodes.
Add a new cluster to the existing instance, and enable multi-cluster routing in the app profile.
Add a new cluster to the existing instance, and isolate the workloads with two app profiles.
Scale up the Bigtable instance by enabling Autoscaling.

questions.explanation:
Bigtable app profiles control how each workload routes requests. To isolate workloads, add a second cluster and use separate app profiles with single-cluster routing so the application-serving workload and batch analytics workload use different clusters. Multi-cluster routing can send requests to any available cluster, so it does not provide that isolation.

**Learn more:** [App profiles overview | Bigtable](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/app-profiles) · [Create and configure app profiles | Bigtable](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/configuring-app-profiles)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are creating a data warehouse in BigQuery. Your data sources include several on-premises MySQL databases. You must move data from those databases into BigQuery for analytics, using a managed solution with low latency that is simple to configure. What should you do?

options.text: Use Datastream to connect to your on-premises database and create a stream. Have Datastream write to Cloud Storage. Then use Dataflow to process the data into BigQuery.
Use Cloud Data Fusion and scheduled workflows to extract data from MySQL. Transform this data into the appropriate schema, and load this data into your BigQuery database.

Use Database Migration Service to replicate data to a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance. Create federated tables in BigQuery on top of the replicated instances to transform and load the data into your BigQuery database.
Create extracts from your on-premises databases periodically, and push these extracts to Cloud Storage. Upload the changes into BigQuery, and merge them with existing tables.

questions.explanation:
Datastream is a serverless change-data-capture and replication service that supports on-premises MySQL sources and low-latency data synchronization. It can write change events to Cloud Storage and integrates with Dataflow templates to load and process those changes in BigQuery, making it the managed low-latency architecture among the available choices.

**Learn more:** [Datastream overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/datastream/docs/overview) · [Datastream sources](https://docs.cloud.google.com/datastream/docs/sources)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You plan to migrate an on-premises MySQL database to Cloud SQL. The on-premises database currently has 16 cores and 64 GB of RAM and averages 75% CPU utilization to support an application with over 100.000 tables.  
  
You need to specify the most cost-effective machine size required when migrating to Cloud SQL for MySQL. What should you do?

options.text: Select a Cloud SQL for MySQL database with a machine configuration of 12 cores and 48 GB of RAM.
Select a Cloud SQL for MySQL database with a machine configuration of 16 cores and 64 GB of RAM.
Select a Cloud SQL for MySQL database with a machine configuration of 32 cores and 256 GB of RAM.
Select a Cloud SQL for MySQL database with a machine configuration of 64 cores and 768 GB of RAM.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL for MySQL has a default limit of 50,000 tables. An instance can support up to 500,000 tables only if it has at least 32 cores and 200 GB of memory. A 32-core, 256-GB configuration meets those requirements and is the least costly listed configuration that does so.

**Learn more:** [Quotas and limits — Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/quotas)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You run a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL 13 Enterprise Edition instance. An audit finds that the write-ahead logs used for point-in-time recovery (PITR) are stored on disk. You need PITR logs to be stored in a Cloud Storage bucket going forward. How can you do this without reducing recoverability or losing the existing PITR logs?

options.text: Clone the instance. Create a new instance with PITR retention set to 30 days.
Change the transaction logs (WAL) retention period.
Upgrade to Enterprise Plus Edition.
Disable PITR, then enable PITR.

questions.explanation:
For an eligible Cloud SQL Enterprise instance, an in-place upgrade to Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus automatically changes the storage location of PITR write-ahead logs from disk to Cloud Storage. This transition preserves the PITR process, whereas disabling PITR breaks the current transaction-log chain and changing retention only changes how long logs are kept.

**Learn more:** [Configure point-in-time recovery (PITR) | Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/backup-recovery/configure-pitr?hl=en) · [Upgrade an instance to Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus edition by using in-place upgrade](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/upgrade-cloud-sql-instance-to-enterprise-plus-in-place?hl=en)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A retail organization is preparing for the holiday season. Catalog-service usage is increasing, and the DevOps team supports the Cloud SQL databases powering a microservices-based application. The DevOps team has added instrumentation by using Sqlcommenter. You need to determine the root cause of certain failing microservice calls. What should you do?

options.text: Watch Query Insights for long running queries.
Watch the Cloud SQL instance monitor for CPU utilization metrics.
Watch the Cloud SQL recommenders for overprovisioned instances.
Watch Cloud Trace for application requests that are failing.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Trace provides distributed, end-to-end tracing for application requests in a microservices architecture and is intended to help troubleshoot failures. Sqlcommenter can propagate application and trace-context information with SQL queries, allowing database activity to be correlated with the failing request path.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Trace overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/trace/docs/overview) · [Cloud SQL database observability](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/observability)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: You manage a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance in Google Cloud. You need to test your Cloud SQL instance’s high availability by performing a failover. You want to use the cloud command. What should you do?

options.text: Use gcloud sql instances failover <PrimaryInstanceName>.
Use gcloud sql instances failover <ReplicaInstanceName>.
Use gcloud sql instances promote-replica <PrimaryInstanceName>.
Use gcloud sql instances promote-replica <ReplicaInstanceName>.

questions.explanation:
A manual high-availability failover is initiated with `gcloud sql instances failover` and the primary Cloud SQL instance ID. The command triggers failover to the standby; `promote-replica` is for promoting a read replica rather than testing HA failover.\
\
**Learn more:** [gcloud sql instances failover](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/sql/instances/failover)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud

options.text: For each application code, set up a common shared user account.

questions.question: You manage multiple applications that connect to a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL database. You need to monitor database performance so that you can easily identify applications with long-running, resource-intensive queries. What should you do?

options.text: Use log messages produced by Cloud SQL.
Use Query Insights for Cloud SQL.
Use the Cloud Monitoring dashboard with available metrics from Cloud SQL.
Use Cloud SQL instance monitoring in the Google Cloud Console.

questions.explanation:
Query Insights provides application-centric monitoring for Cloud SQL query performance. It can break down database load using query and application-tag data, including execution time and CPU, I/O, and lock waits, so resource-intensive or long-running queries can be traced to the applications that issue them.\
\
**Learn more:** [Use Query Insights to improve query performance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/using-query-insights)

questions.question: You manage multiple applications that connect to a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL database. You need to monitor database performance so that you can easily identify applications with long-running, resource-intensive queries. What should you do?

options.text: Reuse the existing service account that populates this database.
Create a new service account, and grant it the Cloud Spanner Database Admin role.
Create a new service account, and grant it the Cloud Spanner Database Reader role.
Create a new service account, and grant it the spanner.databases.select permission.

questions.explanation:
A separate service account isolates this application's identity, and the predefined Cloud Spanner Database Reader role follows least privilege by allowing database reads and SQL queries without write or administrative capabilities. The role also includes the supporting permissions required for read-only database access; granting only `spanner.databases.select` does not provide the complete permission set needed by a typical Spanner client.

**Learn more:** [IAM overview | Spanner](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/iam)
