Your Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL database that supports a financial application has been seeing “deadlock detected” errors during end-of-month processing. CPU utilization rises to 90% during these periods, and several long-running queries consume significant resources. You need to identify the particular queries causing the deadlocks and implement monitoring to address similar issues before they result in application failures.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud SQL System Insights to identify long-running queries and number of deadlocks that occurred in the database. Enable a log_lock_waits flag to determine if lock waits are causing poor performance. Set up Cloud Monitoring alerts for higher CPU utilization and connection count.
Optimize SQL queries by adding appropriate indexes to frequently accessed columns and rewriting complex joins to use LEFT JOIN instead of INNER JOIN, where applicable.

Implement connection pooling at the application layer to reduce the number of direct database connections and optimize shared_buffers and work_mem parameters in Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL to improve query execution efficiency.
Increase the deadlock_timeout parameter on the Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance. Export logs to Cloud Logging, and create log-based metrics to track deadlock occurrences.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL System Insights includes CPU utilization and PostgreSQL deadlock-count metrics, and query-performance insights can reveal high-load and long-running queries. The `log_lock_waits` database flag records lock-wait information needed to investigate contention. Cloud Monitoring alerts for elevated CPU utilization and connection count provide early warning of the capacity and concurrency conditions that can accompany deadlocks.

**Learn more:** [Use system insights to improve system performance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/use-system-insights?hl=en) · [Use query insights to improve query performance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/using-query-insights)

You need to redesign the architecture of an application that currently uses Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL. Its users report slow query response times. You want to improve the application architecture to provide sub-millisecond query latency. What should you do?

options.text: Configure Firestore, and modify your application to offload queries.
Configure Bigtable, and modify your application to offload queries.
Configure Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL read replicas to offload queries.
Configure Memorystore, and modify your application to offload queries.

questions.explanation:
Memorystore provides a managed in-memory data store for application caching with sub-millisecond data access. Offloading appropriate frequently accessed queries from Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL to Memorystore avoids the latency of querying the relational database for those cached results.

**Learn more:** [Memorystore for Redis overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/memorystore/docs/redis/memorystore-for-redis-overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are operating a mission-critical application on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) and use private IP to connect to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL in `us-central1`. You want to maximize database uptime, without making major application changes, for a planned event such as maintenance. What should you do?

options.text: Enable Automated backups and configure the retention period to 365 days.
Create a cross-region read replica in us-south1.
Upgrade to the Cloud SAL Enterprise Plus edition.
Set up notifications about upcoming maintenance sent to your email at least one week before maintenance is scheduled.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus edition provides near-zero downtime for planned operations, including maintenance, on primary instances without requiring application changes or proxy requirements. This directly minimizes maintenance-related interruption for a mission-critical PostgreSQL workload.

**Learn more:** [Availability in Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/availability)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are selecting a database backend for a new application. The application will ingest data points from IoT sensors. You must ensure that the application can scale to millions of requests per second with sub-10ms latency and retain up to 100 TB of history. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud SQL with read replicas for throughput.
Use Firestore, and rely on automatic serverless scaling.
Use Memorystore for Memcached, and add nodes as necessary to achieve the required throughput.
Use Bigtable, and add nodes as necessary to achieve the required throughput.

questions.explanation:
Bigtable is a low-latency, horizontally scalable wide-column database suited to large time-series and IoT workloads. It supports terabyte-to-petabyte data volumes and scales throughput by adding cluster nodes; SSD nodes can provide less than 5 ms latency under appropriate workload and schema conditions.

**Learn more:** [Bigtable overview](https://cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/overview) · [Bigtable editions overview](https://cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/editions-overview)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company is closing its data center and migrating several MySQL and PostgreSQL databases to Google Cloud. The database operations team is severely constrained by ongoing production releases and has insufficient capacity for additional on-premises backups. You need to ensure the scheduled migrations occur with minimal downtime and that the Google Cloud databases remain synchronized with on-premises data changes until the applications can cut over. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use Database Migration Service to migrate the databases to Cloud SQL.
Use a cross-region read replica to migrate the databases to Cloud SQL.
Use replication from an external server to migrate the databases to Cloud SQL.
Use an external read replica to migrate the databases to Cloud SQL.
Use a read replica to migrate the databases to Cloud SQL.

questions.explanation:
Database Migration Service performs minimal-downtime migrations by taking an initial snapshot and continuously replicating source changes until cutover. Cloud SQL replication from an external server likewise supports self-managed MySQL and PostgreSQL sources, maintaining replication to a Cloud SQL replica so the destination stays current before it is promoted for the application cutover.

**Learn more:** [Database Migration Service overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/overview) · [About replicating from an external server — Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/replication/external-server)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An application is hosted in Google Cloud in a single region and uses Cloud SQL for transactional data. Most users are in the same time zone and expect the application to be available 7 days a week, from 6 AM to 10 PM. You need regular maintenance updates for the Cloud SQL instance without causing downtime for users. What should you do?

options.text: Configure a maintenance window during a period when no users will be on the system. Control the order of update by setting non-production instances to earlier and production instances to later.
Create your database with one primary node and one read replica in the region.
Enable maintenance notifications for users, and reschedule maintenance activities to a specific time after notifications have been sent.
Configure your Cloud SQL instance with high availability enabled.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL maintenance updates can require an instance restart and therefore brief downtime. A maintenance window lets the instance be updated during the least disruptive period, so scheduling it outside the 6 AM–10 PM user-availability period avoids downtime for users. High availability primarily protects against zonal or instance failures rather than selecting the time for planned maintenance.

**Learn more:** [Cloud SQL overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/introduction) · [View and set maintenance windows for Cloud SQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/set-maintenance-window)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You administer a production MySQL database on Cloud SQL for a retail company. You conduct routine maintenance at midnight on Sundays, when traffic is low, but want to avoid routine maintenance during the year-end holiday shopping season. You must ensure that the production system remains available 24/7 throughout the holidays. What should you do?

options.text: Define a maintenance window on Sundays between 12 AM and 1 AM, and deny maintenance periods between November 1 and January 15.
Define a maintenance window on Sundays between 12 AM and 5 AM, and deny maintenance periods between November 1 and February 15.
Build a Cloud Composer job to start a maintenance window on Sundays between 12 AM and 1AM, and deny maintenance periods between November 1 and January 15.
Create a Cloud Scheduler job to start maintenance at 12 AM on Sundays. Pause the Cloud Scheduler job between November 1 and January 15.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL lets an instance use a one-hour maintenance window and a deny maintenance period, which overrides the maintenance window for the blocked dates. Configuring Sunday from 12 AM to 1 AM and denying maintenance from November 1 through January 15 schedules maintenance during low traffic while preventing automatic maintenance during the holiday season. Deny periods can last up to 90 days.

**Learn more:** [Maintenance updates on Cloud SQL instances — Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/maintenance) · [View and set maintenance windows — Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/set-maintenance-window)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a transactional PostgreSQL system that is being overwhelmed by analytic queries during the work day. You want to shift this workload to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL and need the most cost-effective solution that supports both the transactional and analytic workloads with minimal downtime.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Define a primary instance for the transactional workload and a small read pool instance that you scale up when the read pool instance is over 80% CPU busy for the analytic workload.
Define a large primary instance to accommodate the transactional and analytic workloads.
Define a primary instance for the transactional workload and a small read pool that you scale out before the work day starts and scale back at night for the analytic workload.
Define a primary instance for the transactional workload, and a large read pool instance for the analytic workload.

questions.explanation:
An AlloyDB primary instance provides read/write access for the transactional workload, while a read pool provides read-only capacity for analytic queries. A read pool can be horizontally scaled by changing its node count without instance-level downtime; increasing the node count leaves client connections unaffected. Scheduling scale-out before the predictable work-day analytics peak and scaling back at night provides the needed capacity only when it is needed, reducing compute cost.

**Learn more:** [Scale an instance | AlloyDB for PostgreSQL](https://cloud.google.com/alloydb/docs/instance-read-pool-scale) · [AlloyDB for PostgreSQL pricing](https://cloud.google.com/alloydb/pricing)

You are planning to migrate a 10 TB relational database from an on-premises environment to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL. The database holds sensitive customer information. You want to follow Google-recommended practices to keep data secure throughout the migration. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Configure Cloud SQL for automatic patching, and enable binary logging.
Establish a Private Service Connect connection between your on-premises environment and the Cloud SQL instance.
Use an external IP address for the Cloud SQL instance, and configure firewall rules.
Set up Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles to restrict access with Cloud SQL with an internal IP address.
Leverage Storage Transfer Service with client-side encryption.

questions.explanation:
Private Service Connect enables private connectivity to Cloud SQL rather than exposing database traffic through a public endpoint. Cloud SQL security guidance recommends private IP when public access is not required, and IAM roles support least-privilege control over who can access and administer Cloud SQL resources.

**Learn more:** [Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL: General best practices](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/best-practices) · [Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL: Private Service Connect overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/about-private-service-connect)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are migrating an on-premises application to Compute Engine and Cloud SQL. The application VMs will reside in their own project, separate from the project containing the Cloud SQL instances. What should you do to configure the networks?

options.text: Create a new VPC network in each project, and use VPC Network Peering to connect the two together.
Create a Shared VPC that both the application VMs and Cloud SQL instances will use.
Use the default networks, and leverage Cloud VPN to connect the two together.
Place both the application VMs and the Cloud SQL instances in the default network of each project.

questions.explanation:
Shared VPC allows resources in multiple service projects to use one common VPC network and communicate through internal IP addresses. Cloud SQL supports private IP in a Shared VPC, enabling Compute Engine VMs in one project and Cloud SQL instances in another project to use that shared network. VPC Network Peering is non-transitive and does not provide the required cross-project Cloud SQL private-IP architecture.

**Learn more:** [Shared VPC overview](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/shared-vpc) · [Cloud SQL private IP networking](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/private-ip)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company is migrating one of its monolithic applications to a microservices architecture on Google Cloud. The new architecture includes a user authentication service running on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) that must access Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instances. Your developers also require database access for local development and debugging.  
  
You need to design a centralized, secure, and scalable database connectivity and access-management strategy for both application service interfaces and developers. What should you do?

options.text: Configure the GKE and Compute Engine applications to use the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy for all database connections. Instruct developers to use their local clients with database-native user/password authentication.

Enable public IP addresses for all database instances and configure firewall rules to restrict access based on the source IP addresses of the GKE cluster, Compute Engine VMs, and developers’ machines.

For all service interfaces and developers, create unique database-native user and password credentials directly on each database instance, and store the credentials in a centralized secret management tool.

For GKE and Compute Engine services, create and grant dedicated IAM service accounts with least-privilege roles for Cloud SQL resources, and configure applications to use workload identity account credentials. For developers, use IAM authentication with Cloud SQL Auth Proxy for secure access.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL IAM database authentication centralizes user and service identity management in IAM and uses short-lived access tokens rather than static database passwords. The Cloud SQL Auth Proxy supports automatic IAM database authentication and provides encrypted, IAM-authorized connections. Dedicated least-privilege service accounts accessed through GKE Workload Identity avoid distributing long-lived credentials to workloads, while developers can use their individual IAM identities with the proxy for secure access.

**Learn more:** [IAM authentication | Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/iam-authentication) · [About the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy | Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/sql-proxy)

Your organization is updating an existing corporate application running in another public cloud so that it can access managed database services in Google Cloud. The application will stay in the other public cloud while the database is migrated to Google Cloud. You want to follow Google-recommended authentication practices and minimize user disruption during the migration. What should you do?

options.text: Use workload identity federation to impersonate a service account.
Ask existing users to set their Google password to match their corporate password.
Migrate the application to Google Cloud, and use Identity and Access Management (IAM).
Use Google Workspace Password Sync to replicate passwords into Google Cloud.

questions.explanation:
Workload Identity Federation lets a workload running outside Google Cloud use credentials from its external environment to obtain short-lived Google Cloud credentials and impersonate a service account. This avoids service account keys and preserves the application’s existing external-cloud identity model, minimizing disruption while it accesses Google Cloud resources.

**Learn more:** [Workload Identity Federation](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/workload-identity-federation) · [Service account impersonation](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/service-account-impersonation)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team operates thousands of connected IoT devices to collect device-maintenance data for your oil and gas customers in real time. You want to develop inspection routines and device repair and replacement schedules from insights gathered from the data these devices produce. You need a managed solution that is highly scalable, supports a multi-cloud strategy, and provides low latency for these IoT devices. What should you do?

options.text: Use Firestore with Looker.
Use Cloud Spanner with Data Studio.
Use MongoD8 Atlas with Charts.
Use Bigtable with Looker.

questions.explanation:
MongoDB Atlas supports multi-cloud deployments across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud, horizontal scaling through sharding, and geographically distributed deployments to reduce latency. Atlas Charts provides integrated visualizations and dashboards for deriving operational insights from the collected maintenance data.

**Learn more:** [MongoDB Atlas multi-cloud deployment paradigm](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/architecture/current/deployment-paradigms/multi-cloud/) · [MongoDB Atlas scalability guidance](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/architecture/current/scalability/)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are using Database Migration Service to migrate an on-premises Oracle database to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL. You observe that DML changes for one important production table are not being replicated to the target, while every other table is migrating to the target without errors.  
  
What could be causing this problem, and what should you do to resolve it?

options.text: The Oracle table does not have a primary key created. Create a primary key on the table.
The table has a column of type NCLODrop the column.
Supplemental logging has not been enabled for the database. Enable supplemental logging.
The table is an index-organized table. Change it to a normal heap-organized table.

questions.explanation:
Oracle index-organized tables (IOTs) are not supported for heterogeneous Oracle-to-Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL migrations with Database Migration Service. Convert the affected table to a normal heap-organized table so its data changes can be migrated.

**Learn more:** [Known limitations and recommendations — Database Migration Service for Oracle to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/oracle-to-postgresql/known-limitations)

questions.domain: Design scalable and highly available cloud database solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance containing a product-information table, including a product-description column. Your application development team is building a customer-facing chatbot and wants to find the product that most closely matches a freeform text description supplied by the customer. How should you enable this functionality?

options.text: Create a stored procedure that uses a regular expression to match the customer’s search text to values in the product description column.
Create and populate a column of product description embeddings on the product table and perform an approximate nearest neighbor search using the customer’s search text.
Use the LIKE operator to match the customer’s search text to the product description and return similar rows.
Create a SQL script that compares the product description and the customer’s search text by using the SOUNDEX function.

questions.explanation:
Semantic product matching is performed by generating vector embeddings for product descriptions and for the customer's freeform text, then retrieving the vectors with the smallest similarity distance. Cloud SQL for MySQL supports embedding columns, vector indexes, and approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) vector similarity searches for this purpose.

**Learn more:** [Vector search | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/vector-search) · [Search and filter with vector embeddings | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/search-filter-vector-embeddings)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing a point-of-sale (POS) application for deployment in your retail company’s stores. The application must run on a mobile device while keeping catalog, pricing, and product data current through frequent updates from a central location. Store networks might be unreliable, so the application must operate without connectivity. You want to minimize development time and costs.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a native solution, supporting Android and iOS, by using SQLite, and develop a synchronization API with a central AlloyDB database.
Create a Firebase application with Firestore as the database.
Create a native solution using AlloyDB Omni in the mobile device and synchronizing with AlloyDB in Google Cloud.
Create a web application with Cloud Run and Cloud SQL.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Firestore provides mobile client SDKs with offline data persistence, so the application can read, query, and write locally cached data without connectivity. When connectivity returns, the SDK synchronizes changes with the backend; real-time listeners keep connected clients updated. This built-in synchronization avoids the development and maintenance cost of a custom offline database and synchronization API.

**Learn more:** [Access data offline | Firestore | Firebase](https://firebase.google.com/docs/firestore/manage-data/enable-offline) · [Cloud Firestore | Firebase](https://firebase.google.com/docs/firestore)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A customer runs a global chat application on a multi-regional Cloud Spanner instance. The application recently showed degraded performance after a new application version was released. The customer asks for assistance. During initial troubleshooting, high read latency is observed. What should you do?

options.text: Use query parameters to speed up frequently executed queries.
Change the Cloud Spanner configuration from multi-region to single region.
Use SQL statements to analyze SPANNER_SYS.READ_STATS* tables.
Use SQL statements to analyze SPANNER_SYS.QUERY_STATS* tables.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Spanner `SPANNER_SYS.READ_STATS*` tables provide SQL-accessible statistics for read shapes, including execution counts, CPU time, locking delay, client wait time, and leader-refresh delay. These metrics help isolate the reads responsible for performance degradation and are particularly relevant to diagnosing read latency in a multi-region configuration.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Spanner read statistics](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/introspection/read-statistics)

questions.question:
You are a DBA for a Cloud Spanner instance that has multiple databases. You must grant all application-development team members the following privileges on one specific database:  
  
- Read tables, views, and DDL  
- Write rows to the tables  
- Add columns and indexes  
- Not drop the database  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Assign the Cloud Spanner Database Reader and Cloud Spanner Backup Writer roles.
Assign the Cloud Spanner Database Admin role.
Assign the Cloud Spanner Database User role.
Assign the Cloud Spanner Admin role.

questions.explanation:
The Cloud Spanner Database User role permits reading and writing data and updating a database schema through `spanner.databases.updateDdl`, enabling additions such as columns and indexes. It does not grant `spanner.databases.drop`, so it meets the required restriction.\
\
**Learn more:** [Spanner roles and permissions](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/roles-permissions/spanner)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: You are designing a new gaming application that uses a highly transactional relational database to retain player authentication and inventory data in Google Cloud. You want to release the game across multiple regions. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Spanner to deploy the database.
Use Bigtable with clusters in multiple regions to deploy the database
Use BigQuery to deploy the database
Use Cloud SQL with a regional read replica to deploy the database.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Spanner supports relational data, strongly consistent ACID transactions at global scale, and multi-region configurations with synchronous replication for high availability. It is suited to globally distributed transactional workloads such as player authentication and inventory management.\
\
**Learn more:** [Spanner documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs) · [Transactions overview | Spanner](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/transactions)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: You are designing a new gaming application that uses a highly transactional relational database to retain player authentication and inventory data in Google Cloud. You want to release the game across multiple regions. What should you do?

options.text: Export the data from the existing instance, and import the data into a new instance with solid-state drives (SSDs).
Edit the instance to change the storage type from HDD to SSD.
Create a high availability (HA) failover instance with SSDs, and perform a failover to the new instance.
Create a read replica of the instance with SSDs, and perform a failover to the new instance

questions.explanation:
An existing Cloud SQL for MySQL instance cannot have its storage type changed in place. Migrating the data to a new instance configured with SSD storage is required. SSD storage provides lower latency and higher read/write throughput than HDD storage, which reduces storage-related I/O waits.

**Learn more:** [Choose a storage option | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/storage-options-overview) · [About instance settings | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/instance-settings)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud

options.text: Use advanced DR by setting up a cascading read replica in the us-west1 region, and designate it as the failover DR replica. Test switchover by using the gcloud switchover command.
Create a cross-region read replica, version 8.0.37, in the us-west1 region. Designate it as the failover DR replica, and test switchover by using the gcloud switchover command.
Create a cross-region read replica version 8.0.34, in the us-west1 region. Designate it as the failover DR replica, and test switchover by using the gcloud switchover command.
Create a cross-region read replica, version 8.0.34, in the us-west1 region. Test switchover by using the gcloud promote-replica with failover command.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL for MySQL Enterprise Plus advanced DR requires a directly connected cross-region read replica designated as the DR replica. The DR replica must use the same database version as the primary, so it must run version 8.0.34. A switchover reverses the primary and designated DR replica roles with zero data loss and is the supported operation for testing DR.

**Learn more:** [Use advanced disaster recovery (DR) — Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/use-advanced-disaster-recovery) · [About disaster recovery (DR) in Cloud SQL — Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/intro-to-cloud-sql-disaster-recovery)

You are implementing fine-grained access (FGA) control for your Cloud SQL resources. You want to adhere to the principle of least privilege while retaining centralized control for administrators.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create tags at the project level.
Create tags at the organization level.
Create labels at the project level.
Create labels at the organization level.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL supports fine-grained access control by using Resource Manager tags with IAM Conditions. Organization-level tags provide centralized administrative management and can be inherited by descendant resources, enabling consistent least-privilege access policies across Cloud SQL resources. Labels are resource metadata and cannot be used for IAM allow or deny policy conditions.

**Learn more:** [Access control with Google Cloud tags — Cloud SQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/tags) · [Tags overview — Resource Manager](https://docs.cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/tags/tags-overview)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are responsible for designing a new database for an airline ticketing application on Google Cloud. The application must be able to:  
  
- Support transactions and provide strong consistency.  
- Work with structured and semi-structured (JSON) data.  
- Scale transparently across multiple regions worldwide as the operation expands.  
  
You need a Google Cloud database that satisfies all the application requirements. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL with both cross-region read replicas.
Use Cloud Spanner in a multi-region configuration.
Use Firestore in Datastore mode.
Use a Bigtable instance with clusters in multiple regions.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Spanner supports structured relational data and JSON, provides strong transactional guarantees including serializability and external consistency, and multi-region configurations automatically replicate data across regions with strong consistency. This meets the application’s global scaling, consistency, transaction, and data-model requirements.

**Learn more:** [Spanner multi-region configurations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/instance-configurations?hl=en) · [Spanner transactions overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/transactions?hl=en)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your IoT monitoring platform receives sensor data from 100,000 devices, producing 2 million writes per second during peak hours and 500,000 writes per second during off-peak hours. Each record is 1 KB and uses the row-key format `deviceId#timestamp`.  
  
Your existing 12-node Bigtable cluster has hotspotting in particular device ranges: three nodes handle most traffic while the remaining nodes are underutilized. Read queries generally retrieve the last 24 hours of data for individual devices. Storage cost is also becoming a concern because two years of historical data, totaling 500 TB, is retained.  
  
You need to optimize performance, remove hotspotting, and lower storage costs while keeping read latency below 10 ms. What should you do?

options.text: Implement row key sting wth hash prefix, configure automsted sealing with an optimal min max threshold setting, and migrate data older than 6 months to Cloud Storage.
Split the table by device type, use separate Bigtable instances for different geographic regions, and implement read replicas for query optimization.
Change the row key format to deviceId#timestamp, implement automated scaling with an optimal min max threshold setting based on CPU utilization, and migrate data older than 6 months to Cloud Storage
Increase cluster size to 20 nodes, implement row key salting with hash prefix, and enable compression on all column families.

questions.explanation:
A deterministic hash prefix distributes device key ranges more evenly across Bigtable tablets, eliminating the concentration caused by lexicographically clustered device IDs while still allowing a known prefix and timestamp range for a device’s recent-data read. Autoscaling can adjust node capacity to CPU and storage targets as workload volume changes between peak and off-peak periods. Exporting and retaining data older than six months in Cloud Storage reduces costly online Bigtable storage while keeping the recent, latency-sensitive data in Bigtable.

**Learn more:** [Bigtable schema design best practices](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/schema-design?hl=en) · [Bigtable autoscaling](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/autoscaling)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are beginning a large CSV import into a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance with many open connections. You checked memory and CPU utilization and found that sufficient resources are available. You want to follow Google-recommended practices so that the import does not time out. What should you do?

options.text: Close idle connections or restart the instance before beginning the import operation.
Increase the amount of memory allocated to your instance.
Ensure that the service account has the Storage Admin role.
Increase the number of CPUs for the instance to ensure that it can handle the additional import operation.

questions.explanation:
Too many active connections can interfere with Cloud SQL for MySQL import operations independently of available CPU and memory. Closing unused or idle connections reduces that contention; restarting the instance is the recommended way to ensure maximum resources because it closes all connections and stops tasks consuming resources.

**Learn more:** [Best practices for importing and exporting data — Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/import-export)

Your company uses Cloud SQL for MySQL with an internal (private) IP address and needs to replicate some tables to BigQuery in near real time for analytics and machine learning. You must ensure that replication is fast, reliable, and uses Google-managed services. What should you do?

options.text: Develop a custom data replication service to send data into BigQuery.
Use Cloud SQL federated queries.
Use Database Migration Service to replicate tables into BigQuery.
Use Datastream to capture changes, and use Dataflow to write those changes to BigQuery.

questions.explanation:
Datastream provides managed, low-latency change data capture for MySQL and supports private connectivity to a source database using its internal IP address. Integrating Datastream with a Dataflow pipeline captures ongoing changes and loads them into BigQuery for near-real-time analytics workloads.

**Learn more:** [Datastream overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/datastream/docs/overview) · [Implement Datastream and Dataflow for analytics](https://docs.cloud.google.com/datastream/docs/implementing-datastream-dataflow-analytics)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: Your team is developing a new inventory management application that requires read and write database instances across multiple Google Cloud regions worldwide. The database solution must provide 99.99% availability and global transactional consistency. You need a fully managed relational database backend to store inventory changes. What should you do?

options.text: Use Bigtable.
Use Firestore.
Use Cloud SQL for MySQL
Use Cloud Spanner.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Spanner is a fully managed, globally distributed relational database service that provides transactional consistency at global scale and automatic synchronous replication for high availability. It satisfies the 99.99% availability requirement while supporting consistent read and write transactions across regions.\
\
**Learn more:** [Spanner documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs) · [Spanner product overview](https://cloud.google.com/spanner)

questions.question: Your team is developing a new inventory management application that requires read and write database instances across multiple Google Cloud regions worldwide. The database solution must provide 99.99% availability and global transactional consistency. You need a fully managed relational database backend to store inventory changes. What should you do?

options.text: Use the native export and import functionality of the source database.
Create a database on Google Cloud, and use database links to perform the migration.
Create a database on Google Cloud, and use Dataflow for database migration.
Use Database Migration Service.

questions.explanation:
Database Migration Service manages an initial database snapshot and ongoing continuous replication based on change data capture (CDC), enabling minimal-downtime migrations. It supports MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server source databases and uses native replication capabilities for high-fidelity migrations, allowing applications to continue using a compatible destination database without application changes.

**Learn more:** [Database Migration Service overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/overview) · [Database Migration Service](https://cloud.google.com/database-migration)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are the DBA for an online tutoring application running on a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL database. You are testing the cross-regional failover configuration. The database in region R1 successfully fails over to region R2, and the database becomes available for the application to process data.  
  
During testing, some application scenarios work as expected in region R2, but several scenarios fail with database errors. When executed independently against Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL in region R2, the application-related database queries work as expected. The application works completely as expected after the database fails back to region R1.  
  
You need to identify the cause of the database errors in region R2. What should you do?

options.text: Determine whether the versions of Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL in regions R1 and R2 are different.
Determine whether the database patches of Cloud SQI for PostgreSQL in regions R1 and R2 are different.
Determine whether the failover of Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL from region R1 to region R2 is in progress or has completed successfully.
Determine whether Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL in region R2 is a near-real-time copy of region R1 but not an exact copy.

questions.explanation:
Cross-region read replicas in Cloud SQL use asynchronous replication, so a promoted replica has a non-zero RPO — it is a near-real-time copy, not an exact copy, and the most recent transactions from R1 may be missing. That explains why individual queries succeed when run directly against R2 (the schema and engine are fine) yet several application scenarios fail (they depend on rows that never replicated), and why everything works again after failing back to R1, which still holds all the data. A version (A) or patch (B) difference would break the queries even when run independently, which is not what happens. Option C is wrong because the database was reported available and failed over successfully.

**Learn more:** [Cloud SQL disaster recovery](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/intro-to-cloud-sql-disaster-recovery) · [Promote cross-region replicas](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/replication/cross-region-replicas)

You are the DBA at a large European bank. Your business-critical banking application runs on Oracle 12.2 in an on-premises data center. You have decided to modernize the on-premises Oracle database by migrating it to AlloyDB. You must satisfy these requirements:  
  
- Remain on-premises and preserve open-source portability.  
- Meet data-residency regulatory requirements.  
- Support both OLTP and OLAP workloads.  
- Retain high-availability (HA) mode and automatic failover.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Deploy AlloyDB Omni in a standalone VM on-premises, and set up disaster recovery (DR) in AlloyDB for PostgreSQL.
Migrate to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL by using Database Migration Service.
Deploy Kubernetes-based AlloyDB Omni database cluster on-premises. Enable HA by using the AlloyDB Omni Kubernetes operator, and migrate your Oracle database to Omni.
Deploy AlloyDB Omni as a docker-based container in your on-premises VM, enable HA for it, and migrate your Oracle database to the Omni container.

questions.explanation:
AlloyDB Omni can run in a customer-managed, on-premises Kubernetes environment, preserving local data residency and deployment portability. Its Kubernetes operator creates and maintains standby replicas for high availability and supports automatic failover, which is enabled by default for database clusters. This clustered Omni deployment also supports transactional and analytical PostgreSQL workloads.

**Learn more:** [AlloyDB Omni using the container orchestrator](https://docs.cloud.google.com/alloydb/omni/docs/kubernetes-overview) · [Manage high availability in Kubernetes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/alloydb/omni/kubernetes/current/docs/kubernetes-ha)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage two separate applications: Order Management and Sales Reporting. Both applications use the same Cloud SQL for MySQL database. The Order Management application reads from and writes to the database 24/7, while the Sales Reporting application is read-only. Both applications require the most current data. You must ensure that the Sales Reporting application does not affect the performance of the Order Management application. What should you do?

options.text: Create a read replica for the Sales Reporting application.
Create two separate databases in the instance, and perform dual writes from the Order Management application.
Use a Cloud SQL federated query for the Sales Reporting application.
Queue up all the requested reports in PubSub, and execute the reports at night.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud SQL read replica is a read-only copy that receives changes from the primary in almost real time. Routing Sales Reporting read and analytics traffic to that replica offloads those queries from the primary instance, protecting the continuous read/write workload of Order Management.

**Learn more:** [About replication in Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/replication) · [Create read replicas for Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/replication/create-replica?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization keeps marketing data, including customer preferences and purchase history, in Bigtable. This database is used primarily by data analysts and operations users. You receive a service ticket from the database operations department reporting poor database performance every day from 9 AM–10 AM. The application team has confirmed that its logs show no latency. A new cohort of pilot users testing a dataset loaded from a third-party data provider is experiencing poor database performance, while other users are unaffected. You need to troubleshoot the issue. What should you do?

options.text: Isolate the data analysts and operations user groups to use different Bigtable instances.
Check the Cloud Monitoring table/bytes_used metric from Bigtable.
Use Key Visualizer for Bigtable.
Add more nodes to the Bigtable cluster.

questions.explanation:
Key Visualizer analyzes Bigtable access patterns by row key and time, helping identify hotspots, uneven read or write activity, large rows, and key-range-specific performance pressure. Its time-based heatmaps are suited to isolating a recurring performance problem that affects only the users accessing a particular dataset.

**Learn more:** [Use Key Visualizer](https://cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/keyvis-getting-started) · [Overview of Key Visualizer](https://cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/keyvis-overview)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You operate a toy-sales ecommerce application on Spanner. The application stores details for the various product listings, including name, category, description, and review(s). Your leadership wants customers to be able to ask free-form questions about the product catalog. You want to implement this capability in the easiest, fastest, and least costly way possible.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a Spanner full-text search index. Find the product information or review against the user’s question in a SQL query. Return the response back to the application.
Create, train and deploy a custom ML model(s). Fetch toy details from Spanner and invoke ML predictions from the application layer to return the response.

Register an existing Generative AI Vertex model in Spanner. Use the ML.PREDICT function to supply the model with a user query along with the product information in a SQL query. Return the response back to the application.

Generate vector embeddings for product information in Spanner. Find the vector with the smallest distance between the users’ query and existing product information or review by using the EUCLIDEAN DISTANCE() function in Spanner. Return the closest product information or review.

questions.explanation:
Spanner can register a Vertex AI model and invoke it with `ML.PREDICT` in SQL, enabling a generative model to process a customer prompt together with product-catalog data and return a natural-language response. This avoids the training, deployment, embedding-generation, retrieval-only behavior, and additional application-layer integration required by the alternatives.

**Learn more:** [Spanner AI overview](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/spanner-ai-overview) · [Generate ML predictions using SQL](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/ml-tutorial)

You are a DBA for Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL. You want applications to use passwordless authentication for read and write access to the database. Which authentication mechanism should you use?

options.text: Use Identity and Access Management (IAM) authentication.
Use Managed Active Directory authentication.
Use Cloud SQL federated queries.
Use PostgreSQL database's built-in authentication.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL IAM database authentication authenticates application identities, such as service accounts, with IAM-issued short-lived access tokens instead of database passwords. After the IAM principal is authorized to log in, PostgreSQL privileges can be granted to provide the required read and write access. [Google Cloud IAM authentication for Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/iam-authentication)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are assessing Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL as a potential destination for your on-premises PostgreSQL instances. Geography is becoming ever more important for customer privacy worldwide.  
  
Your solution must meet data residency requirements and provide a strategy to:  
  
- configure where data is stored  
- control where encryption keys are stored  
- govern access to data  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Replicate Cloud SQL databases across different zones.

Create a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance on Google Cloud for the data that does not need to adhere to data residency requirements. Keep the data that must adhere to data residency requirements on-premises. Make application changes to support both databases.
Allow application access to data only if the users are in the same region as the Google Cloud region for the Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL database.
Use features like customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK), VPC Service Controls, and Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies.

questions.explanation:
Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) in Cloud KMS let you control a Cloud SQL instance’s encryption-key location, protection, rotation, use, and access permissions. IAM policies and IAM database authentication provide centralized, role-based access governance, and VPC Service Controls can protect the Cloud SQL Admin API with service perimeters. Together, these controls address data location, key control, and access governance.

**Learn more:** [Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance settings](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/instance-settings) · [IAM authentication for Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/iam-authentication)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are migrating a 10 TB on-premises PostgreSQL database to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL by using Database Migration Service. Schema changes will occur in the source database during the migration. You need to ensure that all schema changes are replicated while minimizing disruption to the ongoing migration.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Make the schema changes in the destination by using the pglogical.replicate_ddl_command PostgreSQL extension.
Make the schema changes in the source by using the pglogical.replicate_ddl_command PostgreSQL extension.
Make the schema changes in both source and destination after stopping writes in source.
Stop the Database Migration Service migration job. Make the schema changes in the source. Restart the Database Migration Service migration job.

questions.explanation:
During a continuous PostgreSQL migration, Database Migration Service automatically replicates DML changes, not standard DDL changes. Running schema changes on the source through `pglogical.replicate_ddl_command` applies them to both the source and destination at a consistent point, minimizing disruption to the migration.

**Learn more:** [Database Migration Service for PostgreSQL FAQ](https://docs.cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/postgres/faq)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You must perform a one-time migration of data from an active Cloud SQL for MySQL instance in the `us-central1` region to a new Cloud SQL for MySQL instance in the `us-east1` region. You want to follow Google-recommended practices that minimize performance impact on the running instance. What should you do?

options.text: Create and run a Dataflow job that uses JdbcIO to copy data from one Cloud SQL instance to another.
Create two Datastream connection profiles, and use them to create a stream from one Cloud SQL instance to another.
Create a SQL dump file in Cloud Storage using a temporary instance, and then use that file to import into a new instance.
Create a CSV file by running the SQL statement SELECT...INTO OUTFILE, copy the file to a Cloud Storage bucket, and import it into a new instance.

questions.explanation:
For a one-time export, Cloud SQL serverless export creates a separate temporary instance that performs the export, allowing the primary instance to continue serving queries and operating at its usual performance rate. The resulting SQL dump is stored in Cloud Storage and can be imported into the new Cloud SQL for MySQL instance.

**Learn more:** [Cloud SQL for MySQL: Best practices for importing and exporting data](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/import-export) · [Cloud SQL for MySQL: Export and import using SQL dump files](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/import-export/import-export-sql)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An application uses a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance. Recently, you have observed performance degradation during peak hours, resulting in slow response times and frustrated users. You suspect inefficient queries might be contributing to these problems. You want to identify and analyze these problematic queries and provide them to the application team for optimization. What should you do?

options.text: Use the underprovisioned instance recommender.
Increase the Cloud SQL instance read_buffer_size flag.
Enable and use Query Insights.
Create a Cloud Monitoring alert based on the database/mysql/queries metric.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL Query Insights is built to detect and diagnose query performance issues. It shows database load for top queries and enables identification and examination of problematic queries, including execution and latency details that support query optimization.

**Learn more:** [Use query insights to improve query performance | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/using-query-insights)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are selecting a new database backend for an existing application. The current database runs PostgreSQL on an on-premises VM and is managed by a database administrator and operations team. The application’s data is relational and receives light traffic. You want to minimize both costs and migration effort for this application. What should you do?

options.text: Migrate the existing database to Firestore.
Migrate the existing database to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL.
Migrate the existing database to Cloud Spanner.
Migrate the existing database to PostgreSQL running on Compute Engine.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL is a fully managed relational database service that retains PostgreSQL compatibility, so it minimizes changes required to migrate an existing PostgreSQL relational application while offloading database administration. Google Cloud supports migrating self-managed, on-premises PostgreSQL databases to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL through Database Migration Service.

**Learn more:** [Cloud SQL overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/introduction) · [Supported source and destination databases](https://docs.cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/postgres/migration-src-and-dest)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You perform daily exports of native BAK files from Cloud SOL for SOL Server to Cloud Storage buckets by using the `gcloud sql export bak` command at 6:00 AM. You want to automate this routine with managed Google Cloud components so that you can focus on other critical tasks of keeping your database healthy and performant. What should you do?

options.text: Enable retained backups for the instance.
Create a Cloud Run function to export with a Pub/Sub trigger. Create a Cloud Scheduler job to trigger the Cloud Run function daily.
Implement automated backups using the console and set the default retention to 7 days.
Create a cron job to export and configure Pub/Sub as the target. Set a recurring schedule of 0 6 * * * for the job.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL does not provide built-in scheduling for BAK exports. An automated managed workflow can use Cloud Scheduler to run daily, Pub/Sub to deliver the event, and a Cloud Run function to invoke the Cloud SQL BAK export operation. Retained and automated backups do not create the required native BAK exports in Cloud Storage.

**Learn more:** [Best practices for importing and exporting data | Cloud SQL for SQL Server](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/sqlserver/import-export) · [gcloud sql export bak | Google Cloud SDK](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/sql/export/bak)

questions.domain: Design scalable and highly available cloud database solutions
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing a new centralized inventory-management system to track items available in 200 stores, each of which has 500 GB of data. You plan to roll out the system gradually to a few stores each week.  
  
You need to design an SQL database architecture that minimizes costs and user disruption during each regional rollout and can scale up or down during nights and holidays. What should you do?

options.text: Use Oracle Real Application Cluster (RAC) databases on Bare Metal Solution for Oracle.
Use sharded Cloud SQL instances with one or more stores per database instance.
Use a Biglable cluster with autoscaling.
Use Cloud Spanner with a custom autoscaling solution.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Spanner is a distributed relational database that supports SQL queries and transactions while scaling out horizontally. Its autoscaling capability can increase compute capacity for higher workload or storage demand and reduce it during off-peak periods to lower cost. A custom Spanner autoscaling solution can set the appropriate capacity limits and scaling thresholds for phased regional onboarding without application-managed sharding.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Spanner autoscaling overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/autoscaling-overview) · [Cloud Spanner Autoscaler tool overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/autoscaler-tool-overview)

questions.domain: Manage a solution that can span multiple database solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage a collection of Cloud SQL databases in Google Cloud. Regulations mandate that database backups remain in the region in which each database was created. You want to reduce operational cost and administrative overhead. What should you do?

options.text: Configure the automated backups to use a regional Cloud Storage bucket as a custom location.
Use the default configuration for the automated backups location.
Disable automated backups, and create an on-demand backup routine to a regional Cloud Storage bucket.
Disable automated backups, and configure serverless exports to a regional Cloud Storage bucket.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL supports automated backups with a custom regional backup location. Selecting the instance’s region satisfies a requirement that backups remain in that same region while preserving managed, automated backup operations. The default backup location is the geographically closest multi-region, so it does not guarantee the specific instance region. [Manage standard backups | Cloud SQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/backup-recovery/manage-standard-backups)

**Learn more:** [Manage standard backups | Cloud SQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/backup-recovery/manage-standard-backups) · [Choose your backup option | Cloud SQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/backup-recovery/backup-options)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization runs a MySQL workload in Cloud SQL. You suddenly observe degraded database performance. You need to determine the root cause of this performance degradation. What should you do?

options.text: Use Logs Explorer to analyze log data.
Use Cloud Monitoring to monitor CPU, memory, and storage utilization metrics.
Use Error Reporting to count, analyze, and aggregate the data.
Use Cloud Debugger to inspect the state of an application.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Monitoring provides the CPU, memory, and storage-utilization metrics needed to correlate a slowdown with instance resource constraints. High CPU or memory use and high disk utilization can indicate that the Cloud SQL instance is overloaded or improperly sized for its workload.

**Learn more:** [Operational guidelines | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/operational-guidelines?hl=en) · [About database observability | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/observability?hl=en)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing an augmented-reality game for iOS and Android devices. You intend to use Cloud Spanner as the primary backend database for game-state storage and player authentication. You want to track the in-game rewards that players unlock at every stage of the game. During testing, you found that costs are much higher than expected, although query response times meet the SLA. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. You need the database to remain performant and highly available while keeping costs low. What should you do?

options.text: Manually scale down the number of nodes after the peak period has passed.
Use interleaving to co-locate parent and child rows.
Use the Cloud Spanner query optimizer to determine the most efficient way to execute the SQL query.
Use granular instance sizing in Cloud Spanner and Autoscaler.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Spanner granular sizing enables compute capacity to be closely right-sized, and Autoscaler automatically adds or removes capacity as workload demand changes. This reduces the cost of idle or off-peak capacity while preserving capacity for workload performance and availability requirements.

**Learn more:** [Autoscaling overview | Spanner](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/autoscaling-overview) · [Compute capacity, nodes and processing units | Spanner](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/compute-capacity)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your application uses Cloud SQL for MySQL. Users run reports against data that requires near-real-time updates; however, the added analytics created excessive load on the primary database. You created a read replica for the analytics workloads, but users now complain about delayed data changes and reports that remain slow. You need to enhance report performance and reduce replication lag without changing the existing reports. Which two approaches should you implement? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create secondary indexes on the replica.
Create additional read replicas, and partition your analytics users to use different read replicas.
Disable replication on the read replica, and set the flag for parallel replication on the read replica. Re-enable replication and optimize performance by setting flags on the primary instance.
Disable replication on the primary instance, and set the flag for parallel replication on the primary instance. Re-enable replication and optimize performance by setting flags on the read replica.
Move your analytics workloads to BigQuery, and set up a streaming pipeline to move data and update BigQuery.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL for MySQL supports secondary indexes on read replicas specifically to optimize reporting-query performance without changing the reporting workload. It also supports parallel replication on read replicas, which uses multiple SQL threads to apply replicated transactions and can reduce replication lag; the documented configuration sequence is to disable replication on the replica, set the parallel-replication flags, re-enable replication, and optionally tune the primary-instance flags for parallel replication.

**Learn more:** [Create and manage indexes on read replicas](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/replication/read-replica-indexes) · [Manage read replicas — Configure parallel replication](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/replication/manage-replicas)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud

options.text: Implement a single-instance Spanner deployment configured for multi-regional data replication.
Deploy an AlloyDB cluster in the primary region with a high-availability instance configuration, and establish cross-region read replicas in another region for global read scaling.
Deploy a single-region AlloyDB cluster with a primary instance and a read replica in the same zone.
Implement a multi-regional Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL deployment with read replicas in different regions, and configure asynchronous replication for cross-region data consistency.

questions.explanation:
AlloyDB provides PostgreSQL compatibility and high availability through active and standby primary nodes in different zones with automatic failover, supporting rapid recovery for the in-region transactional workload. Its cross-region replication creates asynchronously updated, read-only secondary clusters that reduce latency and scale reads for users in other regions, while the writable primary and transactional integrity remain in the required single region. The secondary cluster can be promoted for disaster recovery.

**Learn more:** [AlloyDB high availability overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/alloydb/docs/high-availability?hl=en) · [AlloyDB cross-region replication overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/alloydb/docs/cross-region-replication/about-cross-region-replication)

You are developing an application that lets users personalize their website and mobile experiences. The application will collect user information and preferences. User profiles use a dynamic schema, and users can add or remove information from their profiles. You must ensure that user changes automatically cause updates in your downstream BigQuery data warehouse. What should you do?

options.text: Store your data in Bigtable, and use the user identifier as the key. Use one column family to store user profile data, and use another column family to store user preferences.
Use Cloud SQL, and create different tables for user profile data and user preferences from your recommendations model. Use SQL to join the user profile data and preferences
Use Firestore in Native mode, and store user profile data as a document. Update the user profile with preferences specific to that user and use the user identifier to query.
Use Firestore in Datastore mode, and store user profile data as a document. Update the user profile with preferences specific to that user and use the user identifier to query.

questions.explanation:
Firestore in Native mode is a flexible document database suited to dynamically changing user-profile fields and mobile/web applications. It supports real-time data synchronization, and Firebase provides a Firestore-to-BigQuery integration that streams real-time, incremental updates from a Firestore collection to BigQuery. Firestore in Datastore mode lacks the Native mode real-time and mobile/web capabilities.

**Learn more:** [Choosing between Native mode and Datastore mode](https://docs.cloud.google.com/datastore/docs/firestore-or-datastore) · [Integrate Firestore with BigQuery](https://firebase.google.com/docs/firestore/solutions/bigquery)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage a small Cloud SQL instance that developers use for testing. The instance is noncritical and has a recovery point objective (RPO) of several days. You want to reduce this instance's ongoing costs as much as possible. What should you do?

options.text: Take no backups, and turn off transaction log retention.
Take one manual backup per day, and turn off transaction log retention.
Turn on automated backup, and turn off transaction log retention.
Turn on automated backup, and turn on transaction log retention.

questions.explanation:
Automated backups provide recoverable backup points that can be retained for the required period, satisfying an RPO measured in days. Transaction-log retention is used for point-in-time recovery, which is not needed for that RPO and incurs additional resource and storage cost. On-demand backups are retained until manually deleted, so relying on a daily manual backup adds management overhead and can create unnecessary continuing storage cost.

**Learn more:** [Cloud SQL for MySQL backup options](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/backup-recovery/backup-options) · [Configure point-in-time recovery (PITR) for Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/backup-recovery/configure-pitr)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing a new ecommerce application on Google Cloud. You anticipate high, bursty write traffic during peak sales periods. You need to configure Spanner to maintain consistent database performance throughout this sales period. What should you do?

options.text: Implement sharding to distribute the write load across multiple Spanner instances.
Configure read-only transactions to improve read performance during peak periods.
Use interleaved tables to reduce the number of cross-node transactions.
Enable autoscaling in the Spanner instance, and set the maximum number of nodes to match the peak write volume.

questions.explanation:
Spanner autoscaling automatically increases compute capacity as workload demand rises. Setting its maximum node count to support the expected peak write volume gives the instance sufficient capacity during sales spikes while allowing it to scale down outside peak demand.

**Learn more:** [Autoscaling overview | Spanner | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/autoscaling-overview) · [Performance overview | Spanner | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/performance)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An analytics team must read data from Cloud SQL for SQL Server and update a table in Cloud Spanner. You need to create a service account and grant least-privilege access by using predefined roles. Which roles should you assign to the service account?

options.text: roles/cloudsql.viewer and roles/spanner.databaseUser
roles/cloudsql.editor and roles/spanner.admin
roles/cloudsql.client and roles/spanner.databaseReader
roles/cloudsql.instanceUser and roles/spanner.databaseUser

questions.explanation:
Both viable options include roles/spanner.databaseUser, which grants read AND write (DML) on the Spanner database and is required to update the table; spanner.databaseReader (C) is read-only and spanner.admin (B) exceeds least privilege. For the Cloud SQL side, roles/cloudsql.instanceUser grants the ability to log in to and access the instance so data can be read, whereas roles/cloudsql.viewer (A) only exposes instance metadata and grants no access to the data itself. So D (instanceUser + databaseUser) is the least-privilege pair that actually lets the service account read Cloud SQL data and update the Spanner table.

**Learn more:** [Cloud SQL IAM roles](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/roles-permissions/cloudsql) · [Spanner IAM roles](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/roles-permissions/spanner)

Your company uses a multi-region Spanner instance. The instance holds data for an application that performs many writes without reading the data. You notice substantial latency regression and want to reduce latency and improve performance. What should you do?

options.text: Enable leader-aware routing in the client library.
Add additional indexes to the table.
Disable leader-aware routing in the client library.
Increase the number of Spanner nodes.

questions.explanation:
For blind-write workloads in a multi-region Spanner instance, disabling leader-aware routing can reduce latency. With leader-aware routing enabled, both `beginTransaction` and `commit` can require inter-region communication to the leader-region frontend; when it is disabled, `beginTransaction` is processed locally and only the commit requires the inter-region round trip.

**Learn more:** [Leader-aware routing | Spanner | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/leader-aware-routing)

Your organization operates a production Cloud SQL for MySQL instance. The instance has 16 vCPUs and 104 GB of RAM and runs at 90%–100% CPU utilization for most of the day. You need to scale up the database by adding vCPUs with minimal interruption and effort. What should you do?

options.text: Issue a gcloud sql instances patch command to increase the number of vCPUs.
Update a MySQL database flag to increase the number of vCPUs.
Issue a gcloud compute instances update command to increase the number of vCPUs.
Back up the database, create an instance with additional vCPUs, and restore the database.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL instance capacity is changed by updating the managed Cloud SQL instance configuration. `gcloud sql instances patch` supports patching an existing instance and provides CPU and memory settings for custom machine configurations; changing the machine type can require a restart, but it avoids creating and restoring a separate database. MySQL database flags do not allocate vCPUs, and `gcloud compute instances update` does not manage Cloud SQL instances.

**Learn more:** [gcloud sql instances patch](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/sql/instances/patch) · [About instance settings — Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/instance-settings)

questions.question: Your organization operates hundreds of Cloud SQL for MySQL instances. You want to apply Google-recommended practices to optimize platform costs. What should you do?

options.text: Use Query Insights to identify idle instances.
Remove inactive user accounts.
Run the Recommender API to identify overprovisioned instances.
Build indexes on heavily accessed tables.

questions.explanation:
The Cloud SQL overprovisioned instance recommender analyzes CPU and memory utilization to identify instances that are unnecessarily large and recommends smaller configurations to reduce cost. Its recommendations can be retrieved through the Recommender API, enabling scalable review across a large instance fleet.\
\
**Learn more:** [Reduce overprovisioned Cloud SQL instances](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/recommender-sql-overprovisioned)

questions.question: Your organization operates hundreds of Cloud SQL for MySQL instances. You want to apply Google-recommended practices to optimize platform costs. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Spanner instead of Cloud SQL.
Increase the number of CPUs for your instance.
Increase the storage size for the instance.
Use many smaller Cloud SQL instances.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud SQL best practices recommend splitting a large instance into smaller instances where possible; Google states that many smaller Cloud SQL instances are preferable to one large instance. Separating microservice workloads reduces resource contention and lets services scale independently without migrating to a different database platform.

**Learn more:** [Cloud SQL best practices](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/best-practices) · [Cloud SQL architecture patterns for microservices](https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/microservices_on_cloudsql_whitepaper.pdf)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance in Google Cloud. A primary instance is in region 1, and a read replica is in region 2. After region 1 fails, you must make the Cloud SQL instance available again while minimizing data loss and following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Restore the Cloud SQL instance from the automatic backups in region 3.
Restore the Cloud SQL instance from the automatic backups in another zone in region 1.
Check

Check your instance operational log for the automatic failover status. Look for time, type, and status of the operations. If the failover operation is successful, no action is necessary. Otherwise, manually perform gcloud sql instances failover .

questions.explanation:
For a primary-region outage, a cross-region Cloud SQL read replica provides the disaster-recovery path. Checking `Lag Bytes` quantifies possible replication lag, and checking the PostgreSQL WAL receive/replay positions confirms that the replica has applied all transactions it received before promotion. Promoting the replica in region 2 makes it a standalone read-write primary while minimizing loss caused by asynchronous replication lag.

**Learn more:** [Promote replicas for regional migration or disaster recovery](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/replication/cross-region-replicas) · [Manage read replicas](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/replication/manage-replicas)
