questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company is moving the existing infrastructure for a highly transactional application to Google Cloud. You have several databases in a MySQL database instance and must determine how to move the data to Cloud SQL. You need to minimize downtime while migrating your 500 GB instance. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Create a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance for your databases, and configure Datastream to stream your database changes to Cloud SQL.2. Select the Backfill historical data check box on your stream configuration to initiate Datastream to backfill any data that is out of sync between the source and destination.3. Delete your stream when all changes are moved to Cloud SQL for MySQL, and update your application to use the new instance.

1. Create migration job using Database Migration Service.2. Set the migration job type to Continuous, and allow the databases to complete the full dump phase and start sending data in change data capture (CDC) mode.3. Wait for the replication delay to minimize, initiate a promotion of the new Cloud SQL instance, and wait for the migration job to complete.4. Update your application connections to the new instance.

1. Create migration job using Database Migration Service.2. Set the migration job type to One-time, and perform this migration during a maintenance window.3. Stop all write workloads to the source database and initiate the dump. Wait for the dump to be loaded into the Cloud SQL destination database and the destination database to be promoted to the primary database.4. Update your application connections to the new instance.

1. Use the mysqldump utility to manually initiate a backup of MySQL during the application maintenance window.2. Move the files to Cloud Storage, and import each database into your Cloud SQL instance.3. Continue to dump each database until all the databases are migrated.4. Update your application connections to the new instance.

questions.explanation:
A continuous Database Migration Service migration takes an initial snapshot and load, then uses change data capture (CDC) to keep Cloud SQL synchronized with ongoing MySQL changes. After replication delay has been reduced, promoting the Cloud SQL destination supports a low-downtime cutover. For a lossless cutover, writes to the source must be stopped and replication delay must reach zero before promotion. A one-time dump/load or manual `mysqldump` migration requires a longer source write outage.

**Learn more:** [Types of migration | Database Migration Service for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/mysql/migration-types) · [Promote a migration | Database Migration Service for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/mysql/promote-migration)

You need to migrate your on-premises PostgreSQL database to Compute Engine with the least possible downtime. What should you do?

options.text: Perform a full backup of your on-premises PostgreSQL, and then, in the migration window, perform an incremental backup.
Create a read replica on Cloud SQL, and then promote it to a read/write standalone instance.
Use Database Migration Service to migrate your database.
Create a hot standby on Compute Engine, and use PgBouncer to switch over the connections.

questions.explanation:
A PostgreSQL hot standby on Compute Engine continuously applies WAL changes from the on-premises primary, keeping the destination nearly current. Promoting the standby during cutover and redirecting application connections through PgBouncer confines downtime to the brief switchover period. Database Migration Service for PostgreSQL targets Cloud SQL or AlloyDB rather than Compute Engine.

**Learn more:** [PostgreSQL log-shipping standby servers](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/warm-standby.html) · [Google Cloud Database Migration Service overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are planning a database strategy for a new web application in one region. You must minimize write latency. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud SQL with cross-region replicas.
Use high availability (HA) Cloud SQL with multiple zones.
Use zonal Cloud SQL without high availability (HA).
Use Cloud Spanner in a regional configuration.

questions.explanation:
A zonal Cloud SQL instance avoids the synchronous cross-zone replication required by Cloud SQL high availability. HA commits replicate writes to persistent disks in both zones before reporting a transaction as committed, while regional Spanner writes require a multi-zone quorum. A standalone zonal Cloud SQL deployment therefore has the lowest write-path latency of these options.

**Learn more:** [Cloud SQL high availability overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/high-availability?hl=en) · [Spanner regional, dual-region, and multi-region configurations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/instance-configurations)

You are a database administrator for a rapidly expanding startup that runs on Google Cloud. As the company grows, the Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL database workload is rising exponentially. You need to put in place a proactive approach that continuously evaluates and optimizes the cost of your database solution while ensuring that it satisfies performance requirements.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Set up budget alerts in Cloud Billing to notify you when spending exceeds predefined thresholds.
Implement a combination of automated scripts to analyze usage patterns and Cloud Monitoring custom metrics to track performance. Manage scaling based on defined thresholds.
Use Query Insights to identify and address performance bottlenecks, then adjust instance sizes based on recommendations.
Review Cloud Billing reports every month, and adjust instance sizes based on observed usage patterns.

questions.explanation:
Automated usage analysis combined with Cloud Monitoring performance metrics enables continuous detection of changing resource demand and threshold-based scaling decisions. This maintains required performance while avoiding persistent overprovisioning and unnecessary database cost. Cloud SQL monitoring metrics support proactive responses to application changes and provide insight into instance usage costs.

**Learn more:** [Monitor Cloud SQL instances](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/monitor-instance) · [About database observability](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/observability)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to migrate an existing on-premises application to Google Cloud. The application supports semi-structured data ingested from 100,000 sensors, with each sensor sending 10 readings per second from manufacturing plants. You must make this data available for real-time monitoring and analysis. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the database using Cloud SQL.
Use BigQuery, and load data in batches.
Deploy the database using Bigtable.
Deploy the database using Cloud Spanner.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Bigtable provides low-latency, high-throughput storage that scales for large volumes of semi-structured IoT and time-series data. It is suited to ingesting manufacturing-sensor telemetry while supporting real-time operational monitoring and analysis.

**Learn more:** [Bigtable overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/overview) · [Schema design for time series data](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/schema-design-time-series)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A team operates a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance containing a 5 TB database that must remain available 24/7. Database backups must be saved in object storage with minimal operational overhead and minimal risk to production workloads. What should be done?

options.text: Use Cloud SQL serverless exports.
Create a read replica, and then use the mysqldump utility to export each table.
Clone the Cloud SQL instance, and then use the mysqldump utlity to export the data.
Use the mysqldump utility on the primary database instance to export the backup.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL serverless exports offload the export to a separate temporary instance and write the result to Cloud Storage. The primary instance can continue serving queries and operating at its normal performance rate, minimizing production impact and administrative effort for a large export.

**Learn more:** [Best practices for importing and exporting data — Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/import-export) · [Export and import using SQL dump files — Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/import-export/import-export-sql)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization works in a highly regulated industry where separation of concerns (SoC) and the principle of least privilege (PoLP) are critical. The operations team includes:  
  
- Person A, a database administrator.  
- Person B, an analyst who produces metric reports.  
- Application C, which performs automatic backups.  
  
You need to assign Cloud Spanner roles to the team members. Which roles should you assign?

options.text: roles/spanner.databaseAdmin for Person Aroles/spanner.databaseReader for Person Broles/spanner.backupWriter for Application C
roles/spanner.databaseAdmin for Person Aroles/spanner.databaseReader for Person Broles/spanner.backupAdmin for Application C
roles/spanner.databaseAdmin for Person Aroles/spanner.databaseUser for Person Broles/spanner databaseReader for Application C
roles/spanner.databaseAdmin for Person Aroles/spanner.databaseUser for Person Broles/spanner.backupWriter for Application C

questions.explanation:
Cloud Spanner Database Admin is appropriate for a database administrator. Database Reader grants the analyst read and SQL-query access needed for reporting without the write and schema-update privileges included in Database User. Backup Writer is specifically intended for scripts that automate backup creation and cannot update or delete backups, unlike Backup Admin; it therefore satisfies separation of concerns and least privilege.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Spanner IAM overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/iam) · [Create backups | Spanner](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/backup/create-backups)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company is assessing Google Cloud database options for a mission-critical, global payments gateway application. The application must be available 24/7 for users worldwide, scale horizontally, and support open-source databases. You need to choose a fully managed, automatically shardable database that provides 99.999% availability and strong transactional consistency. What should you do?

options.text: Select Bare Metal Solution for Oracle.
Select Cloud SQL.
Select Bigtable.
Select Cloud Spanner.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Spanner is a fully managed distributed database with automatic sharding for horizontal scale, strong ACID transactional consistency across global deployments, and PostgreSQL support. A multi-region Enterprise Plus configuration provides up to a 99.999% availability SLA, making it suitable for a globally available payments workload.

**Learn more:** [Spanner: Always-on, virtually unlimited scale database](https://cloud.google.com/spanner) · [Spanner editions overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/editions-overview)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing a backup and recovery strategy for a Cloud SQL for MySQL database that supports a write-heavy application. You must be able to restore the database to any point in time during the preceding five days while minimizing the performance effect of database backups. What should you do?

options.text: Enable automatic backup and point in time recovery. Configure the backup window during periods of low database traffic. Set backup and transaction log retention to at least five days.
Schedule hourly on-demand backups and enable point in time recovery. Delete any delete backups that were taken over five days ago.
Schedule a database export job to run every hour from a read replica instance. Retain the export dumps for at least five days.
Schedule a database export job to run every hour. Use serverless export. Retain the export dumps for at least five days.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL for MySQL point-in-time recovery uses automated backups together with retained binary transaction logs to restore to a specific time. Setting backup and transaction-log retention to at least five days provides the required recovery window, and placing the automatic backup window in a low-traffic period minimizes backup impact on a write-heavy workload.

**Learn more:** [Configure point-in-time recovery (PITR) — Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/backup-recovery/configure-pitr?hl=en) · [Cloud SQL backups overview — Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/backup-recovery/backups)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are creating new Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instances in `us-east1` and `us-east4`. Starting with `us-east1`, you are assigning private IP addresses to the Cloud SQL instances so that you can access the instance without using the internet or external IP addresses. However, you repeatedly receive a “Network association failed” error message. You are using a shared VPC network. What should you do to resolve the issue?

options.text: Use the Google Cloud console to assign private IP.
Enable the Service Networking API for the host and service projects.
Configure Private Services Access prior to assigning a private IP to Cloud SQL.
Assign the private IP by using the gcloud sql instances patch command.

questions.explanation:
For a Cloud SQL private-IP configuration that uses Shared VPC, the Service Networking API must be enabled in both the service project and the Shared VPC host project. A “Network association failed” error during private-IP assignment specifically requires enabling the API for the host project as well.

**Learn more:** [Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL error messages](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/error-messages?hl=en)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You plan to migrate an on-premises, mission-critical PostgreSQL database to Cloud SQL. The database must withstand a zonal failure with under five minutes of downtime while losing no transactions. You want to follow Google-recommended migration practices. What should you do?

options.text: Take nightly snapshots of the primary database instance, and restore them in a secondary zone.
Build a change data capture (CDC) pipeline to read transactions from the primary instance, and replicate them to a secondary instance.
Create a read replica in another region, and promote the read replica if a failure occurs.
Enable high availability (HA) for the database to make it regional.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL high availability (HA) configures a regional instance with a primary and standby in separate zones. Writes are synchronously replicated to persistent disks in both zones before commitment, so a zonal failover does not lose committed transactions. Cloud SQL automatically promotes the standby during a zone failure, with expected unavailability of about 60 seconds.

**Learn more:** [About high availability | Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/high-availability) · [Availability in Cloud SQL | Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/availability)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team is developing an application that stores and analyzes streaming financial time-series data. You require a database solution that can run time-series scans with sub-second latency. The solution must scale to hundreds of terabytes, write up to 10k records per second, and read up to 200 MB per second. What should you do?

options.text: Use Firestore.
Use Bigtable
Use BigQuery.
Use Cloud Spanner.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Bigtable is a wide-column NoSQL database suited to time-series data and low-latency, high-throughput workloads. It scales linearly by adding nodes and supports terabyte-to-petabyte datasets. Its documented SSD performance includes up to 14,000 writes per second and up to 220 MB/s scan throughput per node under typical conditions, satisfying the required 10k writes per second and 200 MB/s reads when properly provisioned.

**Learn more:** [Bigtable overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/overview) · [Understand performance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/performance)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company’s mission-critical, globally available application is backed by a Cloud Spanner database. Experienced application users have read and write access to the database, while new users receive read-only database access. You must assign the appropriate Cloud Spanner Identity and Access Management (IAM) role to new users who will be onboarded soon. Which role should you configure?

options.text: roles/spanner.databaseReader
roles/spanner.databaseUser
roles/spanner.viewer
roles/spanner.backupWriter

questions.explanation:
The Cloud Spanner Database Reader role (`roles/spanner.databaseReader`) provides read-only access for querying and reading a Cloud Spanner database. It does not grant the write permissions included in the Database User role.

**Learn more:** [Spanner roles and permissions](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/roles-permissions/spanner) · [Set up your environment — Cloud Spanner](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/getting-started/set-up)

questions.question: You must issue a new server certificate because the current one is about to expire. You need to avoid restarting your Cloud SQL for MySQL instance. What should you do in the Cloud SQL instance?

options.text: Issue a rollback, and download your server certificate.
Create a new client certificate, and download it.
Create a new server certificate, and download it.
Reset your SSL configuration, and download your server certificate.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL supports creating a new server certificate as an upcoming certificate, downloading its CA information, and updating clients before completing certificate rotation. This prepares the replacement server certificate without requiring an instance restart.\
\
**Learn more:** [Configure SSL/TLS certificates | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/configure-ssl-instance)

questions.domain: Design scalable and highly available cloud database solutions
questions.question: You must issue a new server certificate because the current one is about to expire. You need to avoid restarting your Cloud SQL for MySQL instance. What should you do in the Cloud SQL instance?

options.text: Disable and remove the internal IP address assignment.
Disable both the external IP address and the internal IP address, and instead rely on Private Google Access.
Specify an authorized network with the CIDR range of the VM.
Disable and remove the external IP address assignment.

questions.explanation:
A Compute Engine VM in the same VPC can reach a Cloud SQL instance through private IP connectivity. Disabling the Cloud SQL instance’s public IP removes an unnecessary internet-accessible endpoint while preserving the required private VPC path. Google Cloud recommends private IP unless an internet-accessible instance is specifically required.

**Learn more:** [Learn about using private IP | Cloud SQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/private-ip?hl=en) · [Choose how to connect to Cloud SQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/sqlserver/connect-overview)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: A company is migrating an on-premises database to a single-region Spanner instance. At peak, the existing database supports 40,000 reads per second and 7,000 writes per second, with 1 KB row sizes. You need to identify the most cost-effective Spanner instance size that can handle the equivalent current workload. What should you do?

options.text: Select a 4-node Spanner instance.
Select a 6-node Spanner instance.
Select a 1-node Spanner instance.
Recommend a multi-region Spanner instance.

questions.explanation:
A 4-node single-region Spanner instance meets the read requirement of 40,000 1-KB reads per second and exceeds the 7,000 1-KB writes-per-second requirement. It is therefore the least-cost option that satisfies both throughput needs. Spanner throughput scales linearly as compute capacity is added.\
\
**Learn more:** [Spanner performance overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/performance)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have completed migrating an on-premises MySQL database to Cloud SQL. You need to ensure that the daily export of a table—previously performed by a cron job on the database server—continues. You want the solution to minimize cost and operational overhead. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Scheduler and Cloud Functions to run the daily export.
Create a streaming Datatlow job to export the table.
Set up Cloud Composer, and create a task to export the table daily.
Run the cron job on a Compute Engine instance to continue the export.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Scheduler can run recurring cron-style jobs and invoke a target such as a function endpoint. A Cloud Function can execute the export only when scheduled, providing a managed serverless solution without maintaining a Compute Engine VM or operating a workflow or streaming-data platform.

**Learn more:** [Manage cron jobs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/scheduler/docs/creating) · [Schedule an HTTP Cloud Run function](https://docs.cloud.google.com/scheduler/docs/tut-gcf-http)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An e-learning platform runs on a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance (16 VCPUs, 60 GB memory, and 1 TB SSD) that serves users in North America. Its analytics team runs complex reporting queries that frequently consume 80% of CPU resources, causing slow student-transaction response times during peak hours. The current workload includes 8,000 transactions per second, with 60% reads and 40% writes. The reporting queries use `JOIN` operations across multiple large tables with millions of rows and require highly efficient analytical processing. The platform also has sudden spikes in analytical-reporting demand, requiring elastic scaling of read capacity. You need to improve query performance so the analytics team can run reports efficiently without affecting transactional users. You also need to plan for future traffic growth. What should you do?

options.text: Upgrade to Cloud SAL for PostgreSQL Enterprise Edition and route transaction and analytical queries to the primary instance.
Migrate to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL and upgrade the machine type of the primary instance to 32 vCPU. Create materialized views for common analytical queries.
Migrate to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL with a 16 vCPU primary instance and enable columnar engine for analytical workloads, using read pools for query isolation.
Upgrade the Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance to db-n1-highmem-32 and implement connection pooling with PgBouncer to handle increased load.

questions.explanation:
AlloyDB’s columnar engine accelerates analytical SQL operations including large scans, joins, and aggregates. Read pool instances provide read-only, horizontally scalable capacity and can run the reporting workload separately from the primary instance, preserving primary resources for transactional reads and writes. This combination addresses both analytical performance and elastic growth requirements.

**Learn more:** [About the AlloyDB columnar engine](https://cloud.google.com/alloydb/docs/columnar-engine/about) · [AlloyDB for PostgreSQL overview](https://cloud.google.com/alloydb/docs/overview)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company needs to migrate its Oracle, MySQL, Microsoft SQL Server, and PostgreSQL relational databases to Google Cloud. You require a fully managed, flexible database solution wherever possible. What should you do?

options.text: Migrate all the databases to Cloud SQL.
Migrate the Oracle, MySQL, and Microsoft SQL Server databases to Cloud SQL, and migrate the PostgreSQL databases to Compute Engine.
Migrate the MySQL, Microsoft SQL Server, and PostgreSQL databases to Compute Engine, and migrate the Oracle databases to Bare Metal Solution for Oracle.
Migrate the MySQL, Microsoft SQL Server, and PostgreSQL databases to Cloud SQL, and migrate the Oracle databases to Bare Metal Solution for Oracle.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL is a fully managed relational database service for MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server, making it the appropriate managed choice for those engines. Oracle is not a Cloud SQL engine; Google Cloud Bare Metal Solution supports running Oracle database workloads on certified bare-metal infrastructure.

**Learn more:** [Cloud SQL overview](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/introduction) · [Bare Metal Solution for Oracle](https://cloud.google.com/bare-metal)

You migrated a large, query-intensive data warehouse from an on-premises PostgreSQL environment to AlloyDB. Initial post-migration performance is acceptable, but you want to optimize for still faster analytical queries while remaining cost-effective.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use Query Insights to optimize query performance and the data model for AlloyDB’s columnar storage.
Increase the number of compute nodes for AlloyDB to maximize parallelization and raw processing power.
Focus on client-side query optimization in the reporting tool.
Migrate to BigQuery for transactional workloads.

questions.explanation:
AlloyDB’s columnar engine accelerates analytical query operations such as scans, joins, and aggregates by storing selected data in a column-oriented format. Query Insights helps identify the queries that create the most load or take the longest, allowing targeted query and data-model optimization for effective use of columnar storage instead of broadly scaling compute resources.

**Learn more:** [About the AlloyDB columnar engine](https://docs.cloud.google.com/alloydb/docs/columnar-engine/about?hl=en) · [Improve query performance using query insights](https://docs.cloud.google.com/alloydb/docs/using-query-insights)

Your company uses the Cloud SQL out-of-disk recommender to examine storage-utilization trends for production databases during the past 30 days. The database operations team uses these recommendations to proactively monitor storage utilization and take corrective action. You receive a recommendation that an instance is likely to run out of disk space. What should you do to resolve this storage alert?

options.text: Normalize the database to the third normal form.
Compress the data using a different compression algorithm.
Manually or automatically increase the storage capacity.
Create another schema to load older data.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL’s out-of-disk recommender advises increasing the instance storage capacity manually or enabling automatic storage increase when storage-use trends indicate that the instance is likely to run out of disk space. This prevents an out-of-storage condition and potential downtime.

**Learn more:** [Monitor disk availability | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/using-ood-recommender)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You run a mission-critical application on a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL database in a multi-zonal configuration. The primary and read replica instances are in the same region but located in different zones. You must ensure that the application load is divided between both instances. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Load Balancing for load balancing between the Cloud SQL primary and read replica instances.
Use PgBouncer to set up database connection pooling between the Cloud SQL primary and read replica instances.
Use HTTP(S) Load Balancing for database connection pooling between the Cloud SQL primary and read replica instances.
Use the Cloud SQL Auth proxy for database connection pooling between the Cloud SQL primary and read replica instances.

questions.explanation:
PgBouncer is a PostgreSQL connection pooler that can be configured with separate primary and read-replica targets, allowing the application to route write traffic to the primary and read traffic to the replica while reusing database connections. Cloud SQL does not natively load balance ordinary read replicas; its documentation notes that connection pooling can help distribute queries across replicas when used with a load-balancing setup.

**Learn more:** [About replication in Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/replication)

questions.domain: Design scalable and highly available cloud database solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing a database architecture for a global application that stores information about public parks around the world. The application uses the database only for reads, and a centralized batch job updates it each night. You want to choose an open-source, SQL-compliant database. What should you do?

options.text: Use Bigtable with multi-region clusters.
Use Memorystore for Redis with multi-zones within a region.
Use Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL with cross-region replicas.
Use Cloud Spanner with multi-region configuration.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL uses PostgreSQL, an open-source SQL relational database, and cross-region read replicas make read copies available closer to application users in different regions. A centralized primary can receive the nightly updates, which are replicated to those read replicas.

**Learn more:** [About replication in Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/replication) · [Create read replicas for Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/replication/create-replica)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are moving a telehealth care company’s on-premises data center to Google Cloud. The migration plan specifies:  
  
- PostgreSQL databases must be migrated to a multi-region backup configuration with cross-region replicas to enable restoration and failover in multiple scenarios.  
- MySQL databases contain personally identifiable information (PII) and require regional-level data-residency compliance.  
  
You want to configure the environment with minimal administrative effort. What should you do?

options.text: Set up Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring with Cloud Functions to send an alert every time a new database instance is created, and manually validate the region.
Set up different organizations for each database type, and apply policy constraints at the organization level.
Set up Pub/Sub to ingest data from Cloud Logging, send an alert every time a new database instance is created, and manually validate the region.
Set up different projects for PostgreSQL and MySQL databases, and apply organizational policy constraints at a project level.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL supports multi-region backups and cross-region replicas for disaster-recovery and regional-failover scenarios. Organization Policy resource-location restrictions can be assigned at the project level, where they govern location-based resources in that project. Separating the database types into projects allows a restrictive regional policy to enforce MySQL PII residency while allowing the PostgreSQL project to use the cross-region configuration required for recovery, without manual validation or separate organizations.

**Learn more:** [Restrict resource locations](https://cloud.google.com/organization-policy/restrict-locations) · [Organization Policy overview](https://cloud.google.com/organization-policy/overview)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization operates a busy transactional Cloud SQL for MySQL instance. The analytics team needs access to its data to create monthly sales reports. You must give the analytics team data access without negatively affecting performance. What should you do?

options.text: Create a read replica of the database, provide the database IP address, username, and password to the analytics team, and grant read access to required tables to the team.
Create a read replica of the database, enable the cloudsql.iam_authentication flag on the replica, and grant read access to required tables to the analytics team.
Enable the cloudsql.iam_authentication flag on the primary database instance, and grant read access to required tables to the analytics team.
Provide the database IP address, username, and password of the primary database instance to the analytics, team, and grant read access to required tables to the team.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud SQL read replica handles read requests and analytics traffic separately from the primary instance, reducing load on the transactional workload. For Cloud SQL for MySQL, IAM database authentication is not automatically enabled on read replicas, so the `cloudsql.iam_authentication` flag must be enabled on the replica to use IAM identities; database read grants can then limit access to the required tables.

**Learn more:** [Create read replicas | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/replication/create-replica?hl=en) · [IAM authentication | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/iam-authentication?authuser=1)

questions.domain: Design scalable and highly available cloud database solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing a database strategy for a new web application. You intend to begin with a small pilot in one country and later grow to millions of users across a global audience. You must ensure the application can operate 24/7 with minimal downtime for maintenance. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Spanner in a regional configuration.
Use Cloud Spanner in a multi-region configuration.
Use Cloud SQL with cross-region replicas.
Use highly available Cloud SQL with multiple zones.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud Spanner multi-region configuration automatically replicates data across multiple regions, providing geo-redundancy, resilience to regional outages, and up to 99.999% availability. It is suited to globally distributed applications that require continuous operation at large scale. Cloud SQL cross-region replicas require intentional manual promotion, and Cloud SQL high availability is confined to primary and secondary zones within one region.

**Learn more:** [Spanner proof of concept playbook](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/proof-of-concept-playbook) · [Promote replicas for regional migration or disaster recovery](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/replication/cross-region-replicas)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are your organization’s DBA. You supplied developers with a cloned instance of the production Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL database for testing. After the clone was created, the developers find data missing from one of the recently modified tables. What should you do to make sure that all data is included?

options.text: Take a back up of the production database, and restore it to another Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance. Provide access to the new instance to the developers.
Check for missing roles and privileges in the cloned Cloud SQL instance. Grant missing privileges to the developers.
Clone the current production database, and restore it to an earlier point-in-time (PITR). Provide access to the cloned instance to the developers.
Dump the production database to a file. Modify the dumped file to ALTER TABLE to SET LOGGED on tables that were unlogged in production. Reload the data in the new Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL does not preserve the contents of unlogged tables during backup restoration, which can cause data to be absent in a cloned instance. For databases that already contain unlogged tables, the documented recovery method is to dump the production database, change those tables in the dump to `ALTER TABLE ... SET LOGGED`, and reload the data into the new instance.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshoot Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/troubleshooting)

You are designing a write-heavy application. During testing, you find that write workloads perform well in a regional Cloud Spanner instance but slow by an order of magnitude in a multi-regional instance. You want to speed up write workloads in a multi-regional instance. What should you do?

options.text: Place the bulk of the read and write workloads closer to the default leader region.
Use staleness of at least 15 seconds.
Add more read-write replicas.
Keep the total CPU utilization under 45% in each region.

questions.explanation:
For optimal Cloud Spanner multi-region write latency, place compute resources for write-heavy workloads within or close to the default leader region. Write transactions must coordinate with the leader and distributed write quorum, so proximity to the leader reduces network latency.

**Learn more:** [Regional, dual-region, and multi-region configurations | Spanner](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/instance-configurations?hl=en) · [Leader-aware routing | Spanner](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/leader-aware-routing)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization operates a low-latency reporting application on Microsoft SQL Server. Along with the database engine, you use SQL Server Analysis Services (SSAS), SQL Server Reporting Services (SSRS), and SQL Server Integration Services (SSIS) in an on-premises environment.  
  
You want to migrate your Microsoft SQL Server database instances to Google Cloud while causing minimal disruption to the current architecture. What should you do?

options.text: Migrate to Cloud SQL for SQL Server.
Migrate to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL.
Migrate to Compute Engine.
Migrate to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE).

questions.explanation:
Compute Engine supports a self-managed, full SQL Server deployment, allowing SSAS, SSRS, and SSIS to remain part of the same architecture. Cloud SQL for SQL Server does not support SSAS and cannot host or execute SSIS or SSRS packages, so it would require architectural changes.

**Learn more:** [Cloud SQL for SQL Server features](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/sqlserver/features) · [Migrate SQL Server database to Compute Engine](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/tutorials/migrating-aws-sql-server-to-compute-engine)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are configuring a new AlloyDB instance and want users to connect to AlloyDB using their existing Identity and Access Management (IAM) identities. You have completed these steps:  
  
- Manually enabled IAM authentication on the AlloyDB instance  
- Granted the `alloydb.databaseUser` and `ser-viceusage.serviceUsageconsumer` IAM roles to the users  
- Created new AlloyDB database users that correspond to the IAM identities  
  
Users can connect, but report that they cannot `SELECT` from application tables. What should you do?

options.text: Grant the new database users access privileges to the appropriate tables.
Grant the alloydb.client IAM role to each user.
Grant the alloydb.viewer IAM role to each user.
Grant the alloydb.alloydbreplica IAM role to each user.

questions.explanation:
IAM authentication establishes identity and connection access, while PostgreSQL database privileges control access to tables. The IAM-based database users must be granted the appropriate privileges on the application tables, including `SELECT` where required. Google Cloud’s AlloyDB IAM-authentication setup specifically requires a database administrator to grant each new database user access privileges to the appropriate database tables.

**Learn more:** [Manage IAM authentication — AlloyDB for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/alloydb/docs/database-users/manage-iam-auth)

questions.domain: Design scalable and highly available cloud database solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company is rolling out a new globally distributed application with strict requirements for low latency, strong consistency, zero downtime, and high availability (HA). You must configure a scalable database solution that supports anticipated rapid growth and optimal application performance. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Spanner instance across regions for optimal performance.
Implement Bigtable with replication across multiple regions and configure to prioritize data accuracy.
Create a Cloud SQL instance in HA mode with a cross-region read replica.
Create an AlloyDB instance in HA mode with a cross-region read replica.

questions.explanation:
A multi-region Spanner instance provides globally distributed, horizontally scalable data storage with automatic synchronous replication and strong consistency. Its multi-region configurations provide 99.999% availability and place data near users to reduce latency, while retaining external consistency across regions.

**Learn more:** [Regional, dual-region, and multi-region configurations | Spanner](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/instance-configurations) · [Spanner documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are migrating an on-premises PostgreSQL database to Spanner. You need to identify a solution to handle existing integer-based table primary keys. You want to make minimal application changes while also following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Use application generated sequential integer values as primary keys.
Update default primary key values to max(primary_key) + 1.
Use a UUID function that generates UUID Version 4 values as primary keys.
Generate values by using BIT_REVERSED_POSITIVE sequences.

questions.explanation:
Spanner recommends bit-reversed positive sequences for migrated integer primary keys when applications need to retain integer-compatible keys. They generate unique, nonsequential values that are distributed across the positive 64-bit key space, avoiding the hotspots caused by sequential primary-key values while requiring minimal application change.

**Learn more:** [Migrate primary keys to Spanner](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/migrating-primary-keys) · [Primary key default values management](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/primary-key-default-value)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: Your organization handles sensitive data and must manage its own encryption keys. You are working on a project that stores this data in a Cloud SQL database. You need to ensure the stored data is encrypted using your keys. What should you do?

options.text: Export data periodically to a Cloud Storage bucket protected by Customer-Supplied Encryption Keys.
Use Cloud SQL Auth proxy.
Connect to Cloud SQL using a connection that has SSL encryption.
Use customer-managed encryption keys with Cloud SQL.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL supports customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) in Cloud KMS for encrypting customer content at rest, allowing the organization to control the key lifecycle and access. SSL and the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy address data in transit, not encryption of stored database data.\
\
**Learn more:** [About customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/cmek?hl=en)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: You are configuring a Bare Metal Solution environment and must update the operating system to the latest version. You need to connect the Bare Metal Solution environment to the internet in order to receive software updates. What should you do?

options.text: Setup a static external IP address in your VPC network.
Set up bring your own IP (BYOIP) in your VPC.
Set up a Cloud NAT gateway on the Compute Engine VM.
Set up Cloud NAT service.

questions.explanation:
Bare Metal Solution requires a Compute Engine VM to act as a NAT gateway for internet-bound traffic. Cloud NAT by itself cannot provide internet access to Bare Metal Solution servers because it does not support transitive endpoints; it is used with the Compute Engine NAT gateway VM.\
\
**Learn more:** [Set up Google Cloud to work with your Bare Metal Solution environment](https://cloud.google.com/bare-metal/docs/bms-setup)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: You are configuring a Bare Metal Solution environment and must update the operating system to the latest version. You need to connect the Bare Metal Solution environment to the internet in order to receive software updates. What should you do?

options.text: Migrate the databases to Cloud Spanner.
Migrate the databases to Cloud SQL, and enable a standby database.
Migrate the databases to Compute Engine using regional persistent disks.
Migrate the databases to Bare Metal Solution for Oracle.

questions.explanation:
Bare Metal Solution for Oracle lets organizations run Oracle databases on certified bare-metal infrastructure, retaining Oracle RAC for high availability and Oracle Data Guard for disaster recovery. It supports existing Oracle workloads with minimal application changes and connects to Google Cloud through a managed, high-performance, low-latency network fabric.

**Learn more:** [Bare Metal Solution for Oracle](https://cloud.google.com/bare-metal) · [Bare Metal Solution overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bare-metal/docs/bms-overview)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your project uses Bigtable to store data that must never be accessible from the public internet, even when a requester has a valid service account key. You need to secure access to this data. What should you do?

options.text: Use Identity and Access Management (IAM) for Bigtable access control.
Use VPC Service Controls to create a trusted network for the Bigtable service.
Use customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK).
Use Google Cloud Armor to add IP addresses to an allowlist.

questions.explanation:
VPC Service Controls can place Bigtable inside a service perimeter and restrict access to trusted network contexts. It provides a defense layer beyond IAM and helps prevent access from unauthorized networks when valid or stolen service account credentials are used.

**Learn more:** [Overview of VPC Service Controls](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/overview) · [Supported products and limitations for VPC Service Controls](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/supported-products?hl=en)

questions.domain: Manage a solution that can span multiple database solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are the primary DBA for a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL database that supports six enterprise applications in production. You used Cloud SQL Insights to identify inefficient queries and now must identify the application originating those queries. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Shut down and restart each application.
Write a utility to scan database query logs.
Write a utility to scan application logs.
Use query tags to add application-centric database monitoring.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL Query Insights provides application-centric monitoring through SQL query tags. Adding tags lets Query Insights associate database load and inefficient queries with the originating application and relevant application context.

**Learn more:** [Use query insights to improve query performance — Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/using-query-insights) · [About database observability — Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/observability)

questions.domain: Manage a solution that can span multiple database solutions
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for a retail company that uses Cloud SQL for MySQL to store transactional data. You must combine the transactional data with customer behavior information in BigQuery to make real-time sales predictions by using machine learning. You want to do this without incurring the overhead costs of moving data from their respective data stores.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use Datastream to build ETL/ELT pipelines to move data from Cloud SQL to BigQuery. Use BigQuery ML for predictions.
Use BigQuery ML for predictions, and combine federated queries to Cloud SQL.
Refactor the application to simultaneously write data to both MySQL and BigQuery. Use BigQuery to generate predictions.
Extract data from BigQuery into Cloud SQL, and use Vertex AI to generate predictions.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery federated queries can access Cloud SQL for MySQL data in real time without copying it into BigQuery, allowing it to be combined with data already in BigQuery. BigQuery ML supports creating and running machine-learning models with SQL, so it can generate the sales predictions from that combined data.

**Learn more:** [Cloud SQL federated queries](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/cloud-sql-federated-queries?hl=en) · [Model creation in BigQuery ML](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/model-overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You use Memorystore for Redis to cache frequently accessed data and enhance your application's performance. If a complete regional outage occurs, the application will fail over to a different region. You need to ensure that the Memorystore instance in the new region does not begin with an empty cache after failover. What should you do?

options.text: Use Memorystore Standard Tier. Disable read replicas.
Use Memorystore Standard Tier. Configure at least one read replica.
Schedule exports of the Memorystore instance. Specify a dual-region Cloud Storage bucket as the export destination.
Enable Redis RDB snapshots for Memorystore.

questions.explanation:
Memorystore for Redis exports create Redis RDB backup files in Cloud Storage, and those files can be imported into a Redis instance to restore cached data. Standard Tier replication and read replicas provide availability within the instance’s region, whereas scheduled exports to a dual-region Cloud Storage bucket retain recovery data across a regional outage.

**Learn more:** [About importing and exporting data | Memorystore for Redis](https://docs.cloud.google.com/memorystore/docs/redis/about-importing-exporting) · [Import data to a Redis instance | Memorystore for Redis](https://docs.cloud.google.com/memorystore/docs/redis/import-data)

questions.domain: Manage a solution that can span multiple database solutions

options.text: Create a VM in Compute Engine, and run a cron job.
Create a Cloud Composer instance, and create a directed acyclic graph (DAG).
Create a Cloud Function, and call the Cloud Function using Cloud Scheduler.
Create a Cloud Function, and call the Cloud Function from a Cloud Tasks queue.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Scheduler is designed for recurring cron-style work and can invoke an HTTP Cloud Function on a weekly schedule. A serverless function avoids operating an always-on VM, while Cloud Composer would add orchestration infrastructure that is unnecessary for one scheduled report. Cloud Tasks is for asynchronously dispatching individual tasks, not as the recurring scheduler.

**Learn more:** [Schedule an HTTP Cloud Run function](https://docs.cloud.google.com/scheduler/docs/tut-gcf-http) · [About Cloud Scheduler](https://docs.cloud.google.com/scheduler/docs/overview)

Your company is migrating a legacy, on-premises Oracle database to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL. As part of the migration, you must convert the schema and other database code objects, including procedures, functions, and triggers, from Oracle to PostgreSQL. The database migration must be completed with minimal application-code changes and manual intervention. What Google-recommended approach should you use?

options.text: Manually rewrite both the Oracle schema and queries to be compatible with PostgreSQL syntax and semantics.
Use a schema conversion tool to automatically convert the Oracle schema to PostgreSQL schema, then manually rewrite all queries.
Migrate the data directly from Oracle to PostgreSQL without any conversion. Rely on application-level compatibility layers to handle any syntax or semantic differences.
Use Database Migration Service code conversion workspace, then review and refactor as needed.

questions.explanation:
Database Migration Service conversion workspaces perform initial Oracle-to-PostgreSQL schema and code conversion using conversion rules, including support for stored procedures, functions, and table-level triggers. The workspace lets teams review conversion results, resolve issues, and refactor only where necessary, reducing manual effort and application changes.

**Learn more:** [Migrate your Oracle database to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/oracle-to-postgresql/how-to) · [Conversion workspaces](https://docs.cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/oracle-to-postgresql/about-conversion-workspaces)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization runs a high-volume, low-latency sensor-data ingestion system. Resilience is essential, and the workload is anticipated to grow substantially over time. You must design a database tier on Google Cloud that provides faster performance and high availability while following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy multiple Bigtable clusters, shard data manually across them, and set up the application logic for fault tolerance.
Deploy a single-zone Bigtable cluster and optimize the application code for maximum write throughput.
Deploy a single-region Bigtable instance and increase the nodes to maximize data durability.
Provision a multi-zone Bigtable cluster, configure replication, perform an application stress-test, and set up performance monitoring.

questions.explanation:
Bigtable replication creates independent data copies in clusters located in separate zones and can automatically fail over traffic when multi-cluster routing is used, improving availability. Replicated clusters must be sized for both application traffic and replication work; application-specific stress testing and ongoing performance monitoring support appropriate scaling and low-latency operation.

**Learn more:** [Examples of replication configurations | Bigtable](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/replication-settings) · [Understand performance | Bigtable](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/performance)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are migrating an on-premises online transaction processing (OLTP) PostgreSQL database to Google Cloud. You want to lower the administrative effort required for database-maintenance activities, including vacuuming and memory tuning. You also plan to add analytical use cases to this database. The migration must require minimal schema and application changes. What should you do?

options.text: Use Spanner with PGAdapter.
Use Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL.
Use AlloyDB for PostgreSQL.
Deploy a self-managed PostgreSQL database on Compute Engine.

questions.explanation:
AlloyDB for PostgreSQL is fully PostgreSQL-compatible, which minimizes schema and application changes. It manages underlying infrastructure and resource allocation, provides adaptive autovacuum that automatically adjusts CPU, I/O, vacuum processes, and memory according to workload, and includes a columnar engine that accelerates analytical queries alongside transactional workloads.

**Learn more:** [AlloyDB overview](https://cloud.google.com/alloydb/docs/overview) · [Configure adaptive autovacuum](https://cloud.google.com/alloydb/docs/adaptive-autovacuum)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You operate a large, highly transactional, multi-tenant application on Oracle Real Application Cluster (RAC) with shared storage. You need a solution that delivers high-performance throughput and a low-latency connection between the applications and databases. The solution must also support existing Oracle features and make migration to Google Cloud easy. What should you do?

options.text: Migrate to Compute Engine.
Migrate to Bare Metal Solution for Oracle.
Migrate to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)
Migrate to Google Cloud VMware Engine

questions.explanation:
Bare Metal Solution for Oracle is designed to run Oracle RAC on certified bare-metal hardware with shared storage, retain Oracle capabilities such as RAC and related tooling, and provide low-latency access to Google Cloud services. It supports established Oracle migration approaches, making it appropriate for a high-throughput transactional RAC deployment.

**Learn more:** [Bare Metal Solution for Oracle](https://cloud.google.com/bare-metal) · [Plan for Bare Metal Solution](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bare-metal/docs/bms-planning)

You plan to use Database Migration Service to migrate data from an on-premises PostgreSQL instance to Cloud SQL. You need to identify the prerequisites for creating and automating the task. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Drop or disable all users except database administration users.
Disable all foreign key constraints on the source PostgreSQL database.
Ensure that all PostgreSQL tables have a primary key.
Shut down the database before the Data Migration Service task is started.
Ensure that pglogical is installed on the source PostgreSQL database.

questions.explanation:
Database Migration Service requires the `pglogical` package on a self-managed PostgreSQL source for logical replication. Tables should have primary keys so change data capture can fully replicate row updates and deletes; without a primary key, only the initial snapshot and inserts are supported automatically.

**Learn more:** [Configure your source | Database Migration Service for PostgreSQL](https://cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/postgres/configure-source-database)

You operate a regional Spanner instance without an autoscaler that serves a production workload. During an ongoing promotional event, you observed a surge in database write activity. You received an alert that the database is nearing its storage limit. Based on the storage-utilization trend, the database will exhaust its storage in the next few hours. You want to address this issue as quickly as possible. What should you do?

options.text: Create a custom instance configuration and add a custom read-only replica to the Spanner instance.
Increase the compute capacity of the Spanner instance.
Move the Spanner instance to a multi-regional configuration.
Archive and delete historical data from the database.

questions.explanation:
Spanner’s storage limit is based on an instance’s compute capacity, so increasing compute capacity increases the available storage capacity and is the recommended immediate response to approaching high storage utilization. Deleting data may not promptly lower the storage-utilization metric because physical compaction can take significant time.

**Learn more:** [Compute capacity, nodes and processing units | Spanner](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/compute-capacity) · [Storage utilization metrics | Spanner](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/storage-utilization)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team has recently deployed a new version of a heavily used application to support additional user traffic. Soon after the deployment, your production monitoring team alerts you that replication lag between the primary instance and the read replicas of your Cloud SQL for MySQL instances is consistently high. You need to remediate the replication lag. What should you do?

options.text: Identify and optimize slow running queries, or set parallel replication flags.
Stop all running queries, and re-create the replicas.
Edit the primary instance to upgrade to a larger disk, and increase vCPU count.
Edit the primary instance to add additional memory.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL for MySQL replication lag can result when replica SQL processing cannot apply incoming changes quickly enough. Optimizing slow write queries reduces the replication workload, and parallel-replication flags allow multiple SQL threads to apply transactions concurrently on read replicas, helping them catch up.

**Learn more:** [Replication lag | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/replication/replication-lag) · [Manage read replicas | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/replication/manage-replicas)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a large Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance. The database instance is not mission-critical, and you want to minimize operational costs. What should you do to reduce backup costs in this environment?

options.text: Set the automated backups to occur every other day to lower the frequency of backups.
Change the storage tier of the automated backups from solid-state drive (SSD) to hard disk drive (HDD).
Select a different region to store your backups.
Reduce the number of automated backups that are retained to two (2).

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL automated backups run daily, and their retention count can be configured from 1 to 365 backups. Retaining only two automated backups reduces the amount of backup data kept and therefore reduces backup storage charges. Backup storage is charged at the instance storage rate.

**Learn more:** [Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL FAQ](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/faq) · [About instance settings — Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/instance-settings)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your hotel booking company is expanding into Country A, where personally identifiable information (PII) must meet regional data-residency and audit requirements. You need to separate Country A customer data from all other customer data. You want to create a multi-tenancy strategy that manages costs and operations efficiently. What should you do?

options.text: Apply a schema data management pattern.
Apply an instance data management pattern.
Apply a table data management pattern.
Apply a database data management pattern.

questions.explanation:
Regional data-residency for Country A's PII requires the data to physically reside in a specific region, and geographic location is set at the Cloud SQL/Spanner instance level — so only the instance data-management pattern lets you place Country A's tenant in its own regional instance while keeping other tenants elsewhere. Schema (A), table (C), and database (D) patterns all share a single instance and region, so they cannot satisfy per-tenant residency or provide the hard isolation that audit requirements demand. The instance pattern cleanly separates Country A data while still letting you manage cost and operations across the remaining shared tenants.

**Learn more:** [Implementing multi-tenancy in Cloud Spanner](https://medium.com/google-cloud/implementing-multi-tenancy-in-cloud-spanner-3afe19605d8e)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing an Android game that must store data in a Google Cloud serverless database. The database will log user activity, store user preferences, and receive in-game updates. The intended audience is in developing countries with intermittent internet connectivity. You need to ensure the game can synchronize game data with the backend database whenever an internet connection is available. What should you do?

options.text: Use Firestore.
Use Cloud SQL with an external (public) IP address.
Use an in-app embedded database.
Use Cloud Spanner.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Firestore provides offline data persistence for Android clients. The client SDK caches data and local writes while offline, then automatically synchronizes local changes with the Cloud Firestore backend when the device reconnects.

**Learn more:** [Access data offline | Firestore | Firebase](https://firebase.google.com/docs/firestore/manage-data/enable-offline) · [Cloud Firestore overview](https://firebase.google.com/docs/firestore)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have one global application that uses clickstream data stored in a Bigtable instance. The application's users are distributed across North America, Asia, and Europe. You want to lower user latency while keeping costs as low as possible.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create one instance of Bigtable with three clusters in one central region across three zones. Set up a single app profile with multi-cluster routing.
Create three instances of Bigtable, each one in a region in North America, Asia, and Europe. Set up three app profiles, one for each region with single-cluster routing.
Create one instance of Bigtable with three clusters in a region in North America, Asia, and Europe. Set up three app profiles, one for each region with single-cluster routing.
Create one instance of Bigtable with three clusters in a region in North America, Asia, and Europe. Set up a single app profile with multi-cluster routing.

questions.explanation:
A replicated Bigtable instance can have clusters in multiple regions, with data replicated between those clusters. Multi-cluster routing sends requests to the nearest available cluster, providing lower latency for globally distributed users while retaining a single instance and its replicated data.

**Learn more:** [Bigtable overview](https://cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/overview) · [Replication overview](https://cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/replication-overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have recently launched a new product in the US market. You currently use two Bigtable clusters in a single US region to serve all traffic. Your marketing team is planning an immediate expansion into APAC. You need to deploy the regional expansion while implementing high availability according to Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Maintain a target of 23% CPU utilization by locating:cluster-a in zone us-central1-acluster-b in zone europe-west1-dcluster-c in zone asia-east1-b
Maintain a target of 23% CPU utilization by locating:cluster-a in zone us-central1-acluster-b in zone us-central1-bcluster-c in zone us-east1-a
Maintain a target of 35% CPU utilization by locating:cluster-a in zone us-central1-acluster-b in zone australia-southeast1-acluster-c in zone europe-west1-dcluster-d in zone asia-east1-b
Maintain a target of 35% CPU utilization by locating:cluster-a in zone us-central1-acluster-b in zone us-central2-acluster-c in zone asia-northeast1-bcluster-d in zone asia-east1-b

questions.explanation:
For Bigtable high availability with multi-cluster routing, Google recommends an N+2 configuration: if two clusters are needed to serve the workload, deploy four clusters in different regions and spread them across continents. Multi-cluster routing requires capacity for failover; the recommended maximum average cluster CPU utilization is 35%. A four-region deployment across the United States, Australia, Europe, and Asia provides the required APAC presence and recommended geographic resilience.

**Learn more:** [Examples of replication configurations | Bigtable](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/replication-settings) · [Check out how to optimize database service Cloud Bigtable](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/databases/check-out-how-to-optimize-database-service-cloud-bigtable)

questions.question: You use Compute Engine on Google Cloud and your data center to manage a group of MySQL databases in a hybrid configuration. You need to create replicas to scale read operations and offload some management work. What should you do?

options.text: Use external server replication.
Use Data Migration Service.
Use Cloud SQL for MySQL external replica.
Use the mysqldump utility and binary logs.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL for MySQL can replicate from an external MySQL source, including MySQL running on Compute Engine or in an on-premises data center. This hybrid configuration supports multiple managed Cloud SQL replicas for a source server, scaling read workloads while Cloud SQL administers the replicas.\
\
**Learn more:** [About replicating from an external server | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/replication/external-server)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: You use Compute Engine on Google Cloud and your data center to manage a group of MySQL databases in a hybrid configuration. You need to create replicas to scale read operations and offload some management work. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance with high availability (HA) enabled. Configure automated backups of the Cloud SQL instance, and use the default backup location.
Create a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance with high availability (HA) disabled. Create a read replica in the same zone.
Create a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance with high availability (HA) disabled. Create a read replica in a second region.

Create a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance with high availability (HA) disabled. Configure automated backups of the Cloud SQL instance, and use a custom backup location to store backups in a Cloud Storage bucket in the same region.

questions.explanation:
A standalone Cloud SQL instance with automated backups avoids the additional cost of high availability or a read replica while allowing recovery by restoring a backup within the one-day RTO. Cloud SQL stores backups in a geographically closest multi-region by default, so a custom regional backup location in the instance’s region is needed when the data-residency requirement is limited to a single region. Custom backup locations are supported for automated backups.

**Learn more:** [Manage standard backups — Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/backup-recovery/manage-standard-backups) · [Choose your backup option — Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/backup-recovery/backup-options)
