questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a Cloud SQL instance (DB-1) with two cross-region read replicas, DB-2 and DB-3. During a business-continuity test, the primary instance (DB-1) was taken offline and the replica (DB-2) was promoted. The test is now complete, and you want to restore the pre-test configuration. What should you do?

options.text: Bring DB-1 back online.
Delete DB-1, and re-create DB-1 as a read replica in the same region as DB-1.
Delete DB-2 so that DB-1 automatically reverts to the primary instance.
Create DB-4 as a read replica in the same region as DB-1, and promote DB-4 to primary.

questions.explanation:
Promoting a cross-region replica is a one-way, manual operation that permanently breaks the old replication topology, so you cannot simply bring DB-1 back online (A) or delete DB-2 to make DB-1 'revert' (C) — promotion is irreversible. The pre-test topology had the primary in DB-1's region with cross-region read replicas. To restore it you create DB-4 as a read replica of the new primary (DB-2) in DB-1's original region and then promote DB-4, putting the primary back in the original region, after which you recreate the read replicas. Option B only creates a replica and leaves the primary in DB-2's region, so it does not restore the original configuration.

**Learn more:** [Promote cross-region replicas](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/replication/cross-region-replicas) · [PCDE Q96 discussion](https://www.examtopics.com/discussions/google/view/92705-exam-professional-cloud-database-engineer-topic-1-question/)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization’s databases run in Cloud SQL. Due to data-residency regulations, it requires backups to be stored in a particular region. You must also ensure that the databases have monthly full backups retained until the Cloud SQL instance is deleted, together with daily backups. What should you do?

options.text: Schedule automated backups for Cloud SQL with a retention period of 365 days.
Schedule daily and monthly on-demand backups.
Schedule automated backups, and create on-demand monthly backups to custom backup locations.
Create an Organization Policy Service resource location constraint. Schedule automated backups with the retention period of 30 days.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL automated backups supply the daily backup schedule but use rolling retention. On-demand backups are retained until they are deleted or the Cloud SQL instance is deleted, making them appropriate for the monthly backups. Configuring a custom backup location ensures the backups are stored in the required region.

**Learn more:** [Cloud SQL backups overview](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/backup-recovery/backups) · [Manage standard backups for Cloud SQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/backup-recovery/manage-standard-backups)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to migrate a 100 TB on-premises Microsoft SQL Server database to Google Cloud through a 1 Gbps network link. You have 48 hours of permitted downtime for migrating this database. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use a change data capture (CDC) migration strategy.
Move the physical database servers from on-premises to Google Cloud.
Keep the network bandwidth at 1 Gbps, and then perform an offline data migration.
Increase the network bandwidth to 2 Gbps, and then perform an offline data migration.
Increase the network bandwidth to 10 Gbps, and then perform an offline data migration.

questions.explanation:
A 100 TB offline transfer requires approximately 222 hours at 1 Gbps and 111 hours at 2 Gbps, both exceeding 48 hours; a 10 Gbps link has a theoretical transfer time of about 22 hours. Change data capture (CDC) replicates changes continuously after the initial data load, reducing the cutover downtime.

**Learn more:** [About data flow for SQL Server to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/sqlserver-to-csql-pgsql/migration-types-and-phases) · [Promote a migration job](https://docs.cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/sqlserver/finalize-migration)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization enforces strict policies for tracking production rollouts and periodically provides this information to external auditors to satisfy compliance requirements. You need to enable auditing for several Cloud Spanner databases. What should you do?

options.text: Use replication to roll out changes to higher environments.
Use backup and restore to roll out changes to higher environments.
Use Liquibase to roll out changes to higher environments.
Manually capture detailed DBA audit logs when changes are rolled out to higher environments.

questions.explanation:
Liquibase manages schema changes as versioned change logs and records applied changes, providing a consistent, automated audit trail for database deployments across environments. The Cloud Spanner Liquibase extension supports managing and automating schema changes in CI/CD processes, including incrementally applying changes to databases in different environments.

**Learn more:** [Include Cloud Spanner databases in your CI/CD process with the Liquibase extension](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/developers-practitioners/include-cloud-spanner-databases-your-cicd-process-liquibase-extension)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for a large retail and e-commerce company that is beginning to expand its business globally. Your company plans to migrate to Google Cloud. You want to use platforms that can scale easily, process transactions with the lowest possible latency, and deliver a reliable customer experience. You need a storage layer for sales transactions and current inventory levels, while retaining the relational schema used by your existing platform. What should you do?

options.text: Store your data in Firestore in a multi-region location, and place your compute resources in one of the constituent regions.
Deploy Cloud Spanner using a multi-region instance, and place your compute resources close to the default leader region.
Build an in-memory cache in Memorystore, and deploy to the specific geographic regions where your application resides.
Deploy a Bigtable instance with a cluster in one region and a replica cluster in another geographic region.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Spanner is a horizontally scalable relational database that supports strongly consistent, transactional workloads across multiple regions. A multi-region configuration improves availability and global read locality, and placing write-heavy compute resources within or near the default leader region optimizes write latency. This suits relational sales and inventory data while preserving a relational schema.

**Learn more:** [Spanner regional, dual-region, and multi-region configurations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/instance-configurations)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing a new application on a VM within your corporate network. The application will use Java Database Connectivity (JDBC) to connect to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL. Your Cloud SQL instance is configured with the IP address `192.168.3.48`, and SSL is disabled. You want to ensure that the application can access the database instance without requiring any configuration changes to the database. What should you do?

options.text: Define a connection string using your Google username and password to point to the external (public) IP address of your Cloud SQL instance.
Define a connection string using a database username and password to point to the internal (private) IP address of your Cloud SQL instance.
Define a connection string using Cloud SQL Auth proxy configured with a service account to point to the internal (private) IP address of your Cloud SQL instance.
Define a connection string using Cloud SQL Auth proxy configured with a service account to point to the external (public) IP address of your Cloud SQL instance.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL private-IP connections from RFC 1918 address ranges are automatically authorized, allowing a client with network reachability to connect directly to the instance. JDBC authentication uses a valid PostgreSQL database username and password, and `192.168.3.48` is a private IP address. The Cloud SQL Auth Proxy is optional and requires separate client-side setup; applications connect to its local listener rather than directly to the instance IP.

**Learn more:** [Learn about using private IP — Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/private-ip) · [About the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy — Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/sql-proxy)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing a solution that implements a cache to track all products browsed by users on an ecommerce website, using a key-value database. The solution must be able to connect to the database from multiple VPC networks while providing a managed service, high throughput, low latency, strong security, and private communication. What should you do?

options.text: Choose Bigtable and connect using Private Google Access API endpoint(s).
Choose Memorystore for Redis Cluster and Private Service Connect for networking connectivity.
Choose a Memorystore for Redis instance and Private Service Access for networking connectivity.
Choose a Redis instance on a VM in the Shared VPC network.

questions.explanation:
Memorystore for Redis Cluster is a fully managed, high-performance Redis caching service. It supports clients in multiple VPC networks by creating separate Private Service Connect endpoints for each consumer VPC, keeping communication private while enabling access to the same cluster.

**Learn more:** [Networking — Memorystore for Redis Cluster](https://docs.cloud.google.com/memorystore/docs/cluster/networking) · [About multiple VPC networking — Memorystore for Redis Cluster](https://docs.cloud.google.com/memorystore/docs/cluster/about-multiple-vpc-networking)

questions.domain: Design scalable and highly available cloud database solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company is building a 24/7, global, real-time analytics platform that must store and process large volumes of versioned time-series data. You need to design a platform that is highly scalable to handle traffic spikes and provides high availability for mission-critical operations. What should you do?

options.text: Implement a single-cluster Bigtable instance with autoscaling enabled and row key design.
Implement a multi-cluster Bigtable instance with autoscaling enabled and optimal schema design.
Implement a multi-cluster Bigtable instance across multiple regions with replication.
Implement AlloyDB for PostgreSQL to handle the analytical workload using read replica.

questions.explanation:
A multi-cluster Bigtable instance provides replicated clusters for higher availability, while autoscaling adds or removes nodes as workload and storage demand change. An optimal Bigtable schema, including an appropriate row-key design, is essential for distributing high-volume time-series traffic and avoiding hotspots. Google Cloud documents that single-cluster instances are limited to their zone for availability, whereas replication across clusters improves availability and supports failover; it also recommends autoscaling for fluctuating workloads.

**Learn more:** [Bigtable replication overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/replication-overview?hl=en) · [Autoscaling | Bigtable](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/autoscaling)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company uses Bigtable for a user-facing application that presents a low-latency, real-time dashboard. You must recommend the optimal storage type for this read-intensive database. What should you do?

options.text: Recommend solid-state drives (SSD).
Recommend splitting the Bigtable instance into two instances in order to load balance the concurrent reads.
Recommend hard disk drives (HDD).
Recommend mixed storage types.

questions.explanation:
Bigtable SSD storage is designed for high read throughput and low-latency workloads, providing substantially faster and more predictable reads than HDD storage. HDD storage is suited to large, latency-insensitive workloads and is not appropriate for a user-facing real-time dashboard.

**Learn more:** [Choose between SSD and HDD storage | Bigtable | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/choosing-ssd-hdd) · [Understand performance | Bigtable | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/performance)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You operate a 24x7 online travel agency that uses Spanner. Your company offers services for booking hotels, flights, and local attractions, which your partners fulfill. You must enable partners to access their respective booking data for real-time reconciliation and analysis. You need a solution that gives partners secure access and lets them run ad hoc SQL read queries with minimal to no disruption to the existing reservation platform. You also want to minimize costs.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a view for each partner by using federated queries in BigQuery, and grant each partner IAM access on their view.
Use a change stream to replicate data into BigQuery for ad hoc reporting needs.
Batch export each partner’s data as a CSV file into separate Cloud Storage buckets.
Create a view on Spanner for each partner, and grant each partner IAM access on their view.

questions.explanation:
Spanner change streams capture inserts, updates, and deletes in near real time and can replicate them to BigQuery for analytics. BigQuery separates partners’ ad hoc reporting reads from the transactional reservation workload, while its IAM and dataset/view controls can provide restricted reporting access. Spanner IAM permissions are granted at the database level, so IAM alone cannot be granted on an individual Spanner view as implied by the direct-view approach.

**Learn more:** [Change streams overview | Spanner](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/change-streams) · [Spanner change streams to BigQuery template | Dataflow](https://cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/guides/templates/provided/cloud-spanner-change-streams-to-bigquery)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions

options.text: Deploy Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL in a regional configuration. Create a read replica in a different zone in the same region and a read replica in another region for disaster recovery.

Deploy Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL in a regional configuration with HA enabled. Take periodic backups, and use this backup to restore to a new Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance in another region during a disaster recovery event.
Deploy Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL in a regional configuration with HA enabled. Create a cross-region read replica, and promote the read replica as the primary node for disaster recovery.

Migrate the PostgreSQL database to multi-regional Cloud Spanner so that a single region outage will not affect your application. Update the schema to support Cloud Spanner data types, and refactor the application.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL high availability provides automatic failover between zones within a region, while a cross-region read replica provides disaster-recovery capability for a regional failure. Promoting that replica makes it a writable standalone primary in the secondary region, avoiding the slower and less predictable recovery involved in restoring periodic backups. This architecture addresses both zonal availability and regional disaster recovery.

**Learn more:** [About high availability | Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/high-availability) · [Promote replicas for regional migration or disaster recovery | Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/replication/cross-region-replicas)

You have a non-critical business application running on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) in the `app-dev` VPC. You created an AlloyDB cluster with Private Service Access (PSA) and no public IP address in the `db-dev` VPC. You want the application to connect securely to AlloyDB in a cost-effective manner. What should you do?

options.text: Set up a high availability VPN between the app-dev and db-dev VPCs. Connect the application directly to AlloyDB.
Connect by using the private IP address of the AlloyDB cluster directly from the application.
Connect by using AlloyDB Auth Proxy installed in the GKE cluster.
Install a SOCKS proxy in a VM in the db-dev VPC. Install AlloyDB Auth Proxy in your GKE cluster, and connect to the AlloyDB cluster through the SOCKS server and port.

questions.explanation:
Private Services Access does not support transitive connectivity between separate VPCs, so a workload in `app-dev` cannot directly reach an AlloyDB private IP in `db-dev`. For a relatively low-cost, non-critical deployment, an intermediary VM in the AlloyDB VPC running a SOCKS proxy provides the required network path. Running the AlloyDB Auth Proxy in GKE through that SOCKS proxy supplies authorized, end-to-end encrypted database connectivity.

**Learn more:** [Connect to a cluster from outside its VPC](https://cloud.google.com/alloydb/docs/connect-external) · [Choose a connectivity option](https://cloud.google.com/alloydb/docs/choose-alloydb-connectivity)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization is migrating 50 TB Oracle databases to Bare Metal Solution for Oracle. Database backups must be available for rapid restoration. You also need backups retained for 5 years. You must design a cost-effective architecture that achieves a recovery time objective (RTO) of 2 hours and a recovery point objective (RPO) of 15 minutes. What should you do?

options.text: 1 Create the database on a Bare Metal Solution server with the database running on flash storage.2. Keep a local backup copy on all flash storage.3. Keep backups older than one day stored in Actifio OnVault storage.

1 Create the database on a Bare Metal Solution server with the database running on flash storage.2. Keep a local backup copy on standard storage.3. Keep backups older than one day stored in Actifio OnVault storage.

1. Create the database on a Bare Metal Solution server with the database running on flash storage.2. Keep a local backup copy on standard storage.3. Use the Oracle Recovery Manager (RMAN) backup utility to move backups older than one day to a Coldline Storage bucket.

1. Create the database on a Bare Metal Solution server with the database running on flash storage.2. Keep a local backup copy on all flash storage.3. Use the Oracle Recovery Manager (RMAN) backup utility to move backups older than one day to an Archive Storage bucket.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Backup and DR can retain long-term Oracle backups in an OnVault pool and protect Oracle archive logs at a configured RPO interval. Its mount-and-migrate recovery provides rapid database access for low-RTO recovery. Keeping the recent local copy on standard storage avoids the unnecessary cost of an all-flash backup tier while the production database remains on flash storage for performance.

**Learn more:** [Google Cloud Backup and DR for Oracle on Bare Metal Solution](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bare-metal/docs/solutions/oracle/bms-oracle-backup-and-dr)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are setting up a new PostgreSQL database instance in Cloud SQL. Your application team requires an optimal, highly available environment with automatic failover to prevent any unplanned outage. What should you do?

options.text: Create one regional Cloud SQL instance with a read replica in another region.
Create one regional Cloud SQL instance in one zone with a standby instance in another zone in the same region.
Create two read-write Cloud SQL instances in two different zones with a standby instance in another region.
Create two read-write Cloud SQL instances in two different regions with a standby instance in another zone.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud SQL regional high-availability configuration places the primary instance and its standby instance in separate zones within the same region. It uses synchronous replication and automatically fails over to the standby when an instance or zone fails. A cross-region read replica is not the automatic HA standby mechanism.

**Learn more:** [About high availability | Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/high-availability) · [Enable and disable high availability | Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/configure-ha?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage a mission-critical Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance. While your application team is executing important database transactions, another DBA initiates an on-demand backup. You want to check the backup's status. What should you do?

options.text: Check the cloudsql.googleapis.com/postgres.log instance log.
Perform the gcloud sql operations list command.
Use Cloud Audit Logs to verify the status.
Use the Google Cloud Console.

questions.explanation:
For the current status of a Cloud SQL backup operation, use `gcloud sql operations list`, which lists operations for the Cloud SQL instance. The Google Cloud console reports only success or failure after the operation completes, rather than live operation updates.

**Learn more:** [Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL backups overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/backup-recovery/backups) · [gcloud sql operations list reference](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/sql/operations/list)

Your company has deployed a multi-regional, highly available (HA) PostgreSQL database cluster on Google Cloud using Cloud SQL and regional persistent disks. You need to evaluate the effectiveness of the disaster-recovery plan and confirm the system can recover from a regional outage. What should you do?

options.text: Promote the cross-region replica and verify that the application can still access the database.
Initiate a failover test to the HA standby instance and verify that the application can still access the database.
Create a backup of the database and restore it to a new Cloud SQL instance in a different region to test the backup and restore process.
Conduct a chaos engineering experiment by randomly terminating virtual machines in the primary region and observing the system's behavior.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL high availability uses a standby in a secondary zone of the same region, so its failover mechanism addresses zonal or instance failures rather than a full regional outage. A cross-region replica provides regional disaster-recovery capability; promoting it makes it a writable standalone primary in the alternate region, and application connectivity verifies recovery.

**Learn more:** [Promote replicas for regional migration or disaster recovery | Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/replication/cross-region-replicas) · [About high availability | Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/high-availability)

A rapidly growing ecommerce application at your company uses Cloud SQL for MySQL. Performance problems are appearing during peak-traffic periods. You need to make sure the database can support the load while minimizing downtime. What should you do?

options.text: Use read replicas for query offloading, configure automatic failover, and test failover procedures regularly.
Vertically scale the primary instance by significantly increasing compute resources, such as vCPUs and memory.
Increase storage size on the existing instance and implement client-side caching for frequently accessed data.
Migrate to a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL database for better performance during high load.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL for MySQL read replicas process read requests and analytics traffic, reducing load on the primary instance. A high-availability configuration provides automatic zonal failover, and testing failover procedures helps ensure the application recovers correctly when a failover occurs.

**Learn more:** [About replication in Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/replication) · [About high availability for Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/high-availability)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company intends to move to Google Cloud. The existing data center will close in six months. You run a large, highly transactional Oracle application footprint on VMware. You must design a solution that minimizes disruption to the current architecture and makes migration to Google Cloud easy. What should you do?

options.text: Migrate applications and Oracle databases to Google Cloud VMware Engine (VMware Engine).
Migrate applications and Oracle databases to Compute Engine.
Migrate applications to Cloud SQL.
Migrate applications and Oracle databases to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE).

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud VMware Engine provides a managed VMware environment in Google Cloud and supports migrating on-premises VMware virtual machines to a private cloud. Retaining the VMware architecture enables a lift-and-shift migration of the existing Oracle applications and databases with substantially less replatforming disruption than moving to Compute Engine or GKE.

**Learn more:** [Migrating VMware VMs to your private cloud](https://cloud.google.com/vmware-engine/docs/workloads/howto-migrate-workloads) · [Workload VM migration](https://cloud.google.com/vmware-engine/docs/concepts-migration-options)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You must migrate existing databases from Microsoft SQL Server 2016 Standard Edition running on one Windows Server 2019 Datacenter Edition server to one Cloud SQL for SQL Server instance. During project discovery, you find that the on-premises server peaks at about 25,000 read IOPS. You need to make sure the Cloud SQL instance is sized correctly to maximize read performance. What should you do?

options.text: Create a SQL Server 2019 Standard on Standard machine type with 4 vCPUs, 15 GB of RAM, and 800 GB of solid-state drive (SSD).
Create a SQL Server 2019 Standard on High Memory machine type with at least 16 vCPUs, 104 GB of RAM, and 200 GB of SSD.
Create a SQL Server 2019 Standard on High Memory machine type with 16 vCPUs, 104 GB of RAM, and 4 TB of SSD.
Create a SQL Server 2019 Enterprise on High Memory machine type with 16 vCPUs, 104 GB of RAM, and 500 GB of SSD.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL SQL Server SSD performance is governed by both machine configuration and storage capacity. A 16-vCPU High Memory instance with 4 TB of SSD provides the compute and disk sizing needed to reach the required high read-IOPS level; Google Cloud also recommends 4 TB or greater storage and higher vCPU counts when maximizing IOPS. SQL Server Enterprise is unnecessary when the workload does not require Enterprise-only capabilities.

**Learn more:** [Cloud SQL for SQL Server best practices](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/sqlserver/best-practices) · [Choose a storage option for Cloud SQL for SQL Server](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/sqlserver/storage-options-overview)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You run a Cloud Spanner instance as the backend for your ecommerce website. The quality assurance (QA) team has doubled its number of test cases. You need to create a copy of the Cloud Spanner database in a new test environment to support the increased test cases. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Functions to run the export in Avro format.
Use Cloud Functions to run the export in text format.
Use Dataflow to run the export in Avro format.
Use Dataflow to run the export in text format.

questions.explanation:
Dataflow is Google Cloud’s recommended method for bulk movement of data into and out of Spanner. Exporting in Avro format preserves the complete database schema along with the data, enabling the database to be imported as a full copy into a new test environment.

**Learn more:** [Import, export, and modify data using Dataflow](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/dataflow-connector) · [Spanner import and export overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/import-export-overview?hl=en)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are migrating an on-premises database to Spanner. A few tables, each containing a few hundred records, have no primary key in the source database. You need to migrate all tables to the new database while avoiding hot-spotting issues. What should you do?

options.text: Load the data into Spanner, and designate a primary key later based on business need.
Use the GENERATE_UUID() function to generate universally unique identifier (UUID) values with the STRING(36) data type when you do the migration.
During the migration, swap the order of keys so that the column that contains the monotonically increasing or decreasing value is the first key par.
Migrate the tables with no primary key to maintain consistency with source.

questions.explanation:
Spanner requires a primary key for each table and uses primary-key ranges to distribute data. Random UUID values generated with `GENERATE_UUID()` provide uniformly distributed key values, making `STRING(36)` UUID primary keys appropriate for migrating tables that lack source keys and helping prevent hotspots.

**Learn more:** [Migrate primary keys](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/migrating-primary-keys) · [Schema design best practices](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/schema-design)

questions.domain: Manage a solution that can span multiple database solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You run a transactional application on Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL in Google Cloud. The database uses a high-availability configuration in a single region. You have experienced data issues and need to restore the database to its last known pristine state. What should you do?

options.text: Create a clone database from a read replica database, and restore the clone in the same region.
Create a clone database from a read replica database, and restore the clone into a different zone.
Use the Cloud SQL point-in-time recovery (PITR) feature. Restore the copy from two hours ago to a new database instance.
Use the Cloud SQL database import feature. Import last week's dump file from Cloud Storage.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL point-in-time recovery uses backups and transaction logs to restore a PostgreSQL instance to a specified time before a data-loss or corruption event. PITR creates a new instance, allowing recovery of the database state from two hours earlier. High availability provides failover resilience, not restoration of an earlier logical data state.

**Learn more:** [Restore an instance overview | Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/backup-recovery/restore) · [Perform point-in-time recovery (PITR) | Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/backup-recovery/pitr)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company is migrating its MySQL database to Cloud SQL and cannot tolerate any planned downtime during December. The company is also cost-conscious, so you need the most cost-effective solution. What should you do?

options.text: Open a support ticket in Google Cloud to prevent any maintenance in that MySQL instance during the month of December.
Use Cloud SQL maintenance settings to prevent any maintenance during the month of December.
Create MySQL read replicas in different zones so that, if any downtime occurs, the read replicas will act as the primary instance during the month of December.
Create a MySQL regional instance so that, if any downtime occurs, the standby instance will act as the primary instance during the month of December.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL maintenance settings support a deny maintenance period, which prevents Cloud SQL from scheduling planned maintenance during a specified block of days for up to 90 days. Configuring December as the deny period meets the no-planned-downtime requirement without paying for additional high-availability or replica infrastructure.

**Learn more:** [Maintenance updates on Cloud SQL instances](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/maintenance) · [View and set maintenance windows](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/set-maintenance-window)

You are building a physician portal application in Node.js. The application will be used in hospitals and clinics that may experience intermittent internet connectivity. If connectivity fails, the app must be able to query cached data. You need to ensure the application provides scalability, strong consistency, and multi-region replication. What should you do?

options.text: Use Firestore and ensure that the PersistenceEnabled option is set to true.
Use Memorystore for Memcached.
Use Pub/Sub to synchronize the changes from the application to Cloud Spanner.
Use Table.read with the exactStaleness option to perform a read of rows in Cloud Spanner.

questions.explanation:
Firestore provides scalable storage with strong consistency and automatic multi-region replication. Its offline-persistence feature keeps locally used Firestore data in a cache that can be read and queried while the client is offline, then synchronizes local changes after connectivity returns.

**Learn more:** [Firestore product overview](https://cloud.google.com/products/firestore) · [Enable offline data | Firestore in Native mode](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firestore/native/docs/manage-data/enable-offline)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You support a consumer-inventory application running on a multi-region Cloud Spanner instance. A customer has opened a support ticket reporting slow response times. You observe a Cloud Monitoring alert for high CPU utilization. Following Google-recommended practices, what should you do first to resolve the CPU performance issue?

options.text: Increase the number of processing units.
Modify the database schema, and add additional indexes.
Shard data required by the application into multiple instances.
Decrease the number of processing units.

questions.explanation:
For a multi-region Cloud Spanner instance that exceeds recommended CPU-utilization levels, Google recommends increasing compute capacity as the starting point so the instance can continue operating effectively. Processing units measure that compute capacity; adding them supplies more CPU resources and improves the instance’s ability to handle the workload.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Spanner CPU utilization metrics](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/cpu-utilization?hl=en) · [Cloud Spanner compute capacity, nodes and processing units](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/compute-capacity)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company operates PostgreSQL databases both on-premises and on Amazon Web Services (AWS). You are planning several database migrations to Cloud SQL to reduce costs and downtime. You want to follow Google-recommended practices, use Google-native data migration tools, and closely monitor the migrations as part of the cutover strategy. What should you do?

options.text: Use Database Migration Service to migrate all databases to Cloud SQL.
Use Database Migration Service for one-time migrations, and use third-party or partner tools for change data capture (CDC) style migrations.
Use data replication tools and CDC tools to enable migration.
Use a combination of Database Migration Service and partner tools to support the data migration strategy.

questions.explanation:
Database Migration Service supports continuous PostgreSQL migrations from on-premises, Amazon RDS, and Amazon Aurora sources to Cloud SQL. It manages the initial snapshot and ongoing change data capture replication, provides migration status and observability metrics, and supports a minimal-downtime cutover when the destination is synchronized.

**Learn more:** [Database Migration Service overview](https://cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/overview) · [Supported source and destination databases — Database Migration Service for PostgreSQL](https://cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/postgres/migration-src-and-dest)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage a Cloud SQL for MySQL environment in Google Cloud. A primary instance is deployed in Zone A and a read replica instance is deployed in Zone B, with both instances in the same region. You are notified that the replica instance in Zone B was unavailable for 10 minutes. You need to make sure that the read replica instance is still operational. What should you do?

options.text: Use the Google Cloud Console or gcloud CLI to manually create a new clone database.
Use the Google Cloud Console or gcloud CLI to manually create a new failover replica from backup.
Verify that the new replica is created automatically.
Start the original primary instance and resume replication.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL manages read-replica recovery and can recreate a replica that exceeds its configured replication-lag threshold, then start replication on the replacement replica. The appropriate operational check is to confirm that the replacement replica was created automatically; manually cloning the database or creating a failover replica is not the read-replica recovery mechanism. Automatic recreation of lagging replicas must be enabled and configured with an appropriate threshold.

**Learn more:** [Replication lag — Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/replication/replication-lag) · [About replication in Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/replication)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work in the logistics department. Your data-analysis team requires daily extracts from Cloud SQL for MySQL to train a machine-learning model. The model will optimize routes for the following day. You must export the data in CSV format and want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Scheduler to trigger a Cloud Function that will run a select * from table(s) query to call the cloudsql.instances.export API.
Use Cloud Scheduler to trigger a Cloud Function through Pub/Sub to call the cloudsql.instances.export API.
Use Cloud Composer to orchestrate an export by calling the cloudsql.instances.export API.
Use Cloud Composer to execute a select * from table(s) query and export results.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL CSV exports are started with the `cloudsql.instances.export` API and can include a `SELECT` query. For automated exports, Google Cloud recommends building automation with Cloud Scheduler, Pub/Sub, and a serverless function; Pub/Sub provides the scheduled event trigger for the function that invokes the export API.

**Learn more:** [Best practices for importing and exporting data — Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/import-export) · [Export and import using CSV files — Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/import-export/import-export-csv)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are the database administrator for a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance with pgaudit disabled. Users report that their queries are taking longer to run and that performance has degraded over the past few months. You need to collect and analyze query-performance data to help identify slow-running queries. What should you do?

options.text: View Cloud SQL operations to view historical query information.
White a Logs Explorer query to identify database queries with high execution times.
Review application logs to identify database calls.
Use the Query Insights dashboard to identify high execution times.

questions.explanation:
Query Insights detects and diagnoses Cloud SQL query-performance problems. Its dashboard shows database load by execution time and identifies normalized queries with average and total execution-time metrics, enabling analysis of slow-running queries without relying on pgaudit.

**Learn more:** [Use Query Insights to improve query performance — Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/using-query-insights)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization must migrate a critical on-premises MySQL database to Cloud SQL for MySQL. The on-premises database runs a version of MySQL supported by Cloud SQL and uses the InnoDB storage engine. You need to migrate the database while preserving transactions and minimizing downtime. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Use Database Migration Service to connect to your on-premises database, and choose continuous replication.2. After the on-premises database is migrated, promote the Cloud SQL for MySQL instance, and connect applications to your Cloud SQL instance.

1. Build a Cloud Data Fusion pipeline for each table to migrate data from the on-premises MySQL database to Cloud SQL for MySQL.2. Schedule downtime to run each Cloud Data Fusion pipeline.3. Verify that the migration was successful.4. Re-point the applications to the Cloud SQL for MySQL instance.

1. Pause the on-premises applications.2. Use the mysqldump utility to dump the database content in compressed format.3. Run gsutil –m to move the dump file to Cloud Storage.4. Use the Cloud SQL for MySQL import option.5. After the import operation is complete, re-point the applications to the Cloud SQL for MySQL instance.

1 Pause the on-premises applications.2. Use the mysqldump utility to dump the database content in CSV format.3. Run gsutil –m to move the dump file to Cloud Storage.4. Use the Cloud SQL for MySQL import option.5. After the import operation is complete, re-point the applications to the Cloud SQL for MySQL instance.

questions.explanation:
A continuous Database Migration Service migration takes an initial snapshot and then continuously replicates subsequent changes to Cloud SQL for MySQL. Once replication delay reaches zero, the destination can be promoted to a writable primary and applications can be redirected, limiting downtime to the final cutover window.

**Learn more:** [Types of migration | Database Migration Service for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/mysql/migration-types) · [Promote a migration | Database Migration Service for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/mysql/promote-migration)

questions.domain: Migrate data solutions
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You want to migrate a PostgreSQL database from another cloud provider to Cloud SQL. You plan to use Database Migration Service and need to evaluate the impact of known limitations. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Identify whether the database has over 512 tables.
Identify all tables that do not have a primary key.
Identity all tables that do not have at least one foreign key.
Identify whether the source database is encrypted using pgcrypto extension.
Identify whether the source database uses customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK).

questions.explanation:
Tables without primary keys have limited support: Database Migration Service migrates the initial snapshot and INSERT operations during change data capture, while UPDATE and DELETE operations must be migrated manually. A source database that requires customer-managed encryption keys for decryption cannot be migrated unless Database Migration Service has access to those keys. Data encrypted through the `pgcrypto` extension can be migrated because Cloud SQL supports that extension.

**Learn more:** [Known limitations — Database Migration Service for PostgreSQL](https://cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/postgres/known-limitations) · [Debugging and other tools — Database Migration Service for PostgreSQL](https://cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/postgres/debugging-tools)

questions.domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization runs a critical business application with a Cloud SQL for MySQL backend database. The company wants to build the most fault-tolerant, highly available solution possible. You must ensure that the application database can withstand both a zonal failure and a regional failure, with `us-central1` as the primary region and `us-east1` as the backup region. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Provision a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance in us-central1-a.2. Create a multiple-zone instance in us-west1-b.3. Create a read replica in us-east1-c.
1. Provision a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance in us-central1-a.2. Create a multiple-zone instance in us-central1-b.3. Create a read replica in us-east1-b.
1. Provision a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance in us-central1-a.2. Create a multiple-zone instance in us-east-b.3. Create a read replica in us-east1-c.
1. Provision a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance in us-central1-a.2. Create a multiple-zone instance in us-east1-b.3. Create a read replica in us-central1-b.

questions.explanation:
A regional Cloud SQL high-availability configuration provides a primary and standby across separate zones within the primary region, protecting against a zonal outage. A cross-region read replica in `us-east1` provides disaster-recovery capability if `us-central1` has a regional outage; it can be promoted to a primary instance when needed.

**Learn more:** [About high availability | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/high-availability) · [Promote replicas for regional migration or disaster recovery | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/replication/cross-region-replicas)
